units.title: Unit 1 · ESG & CSR Basics
units.description: The core vocabulary every ESG conversation starts with — stakeholders, materiality, CSR, shared value, and what the three letters actually mean.

units.title: Unit 2 · Climate & Environment
units.description: Scope 1/2/3, net zero, and the environmental footprint every company now has to count and report.

units.title: Unit 3 · Human Rights & Supply Chains
units.description: Value chains, forced labour, and the human side of every supply chain — plus CSDDD, the law that turns human-rights due diligence into a legal obligation.

units.title: Unit 4 · Governance & Anti-Corruption
units.description: Corruption, whistleblowing, and how a board is supposed to keep a company honest.

units.title: Unit 5 · Reporting Standards
units.description: CSRD, ESRS, GRI, and the alphabet soup behind every sustainability report you will ever read.

units.title: Unit 6 · Sustainable Finance
units.description: SFDR, the EU Taxonomy, and how money gets labelled 'sustainable' — or doesn't.

units.title: Unit 7 · Claims & Greenwashing
units.description: What a company is legally allowed to say about its own sustainability credentials — and what crosses the line.

units.title: Unit 8 · Context & History
units.description: The institutions, milestones, and history behind everything above.

esg-fundamentals.definition: Environmental, Social, Governance: a framework for assessing a company's non-financial performance.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: ESG stands for Environmental, Social, and Governance. It's shorthand for the non-financial side of how a company operates: its environmental footprint, how it treats people, and how it is governed.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: It's the umbrella term behind almost every sustainability conversation, report, or job title you'll run into.
esg-fundamentals.example: A company's ESG report might cover its carbon emissions (E), factory working conditions (S), and board diversity (G) all in one document.
esg-fundamentals.dontConfuseWith: CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) — CSR is a company's voluntary program of doing good; ESG is the measurable framework investors and regulators use to assess performance.

esg-fundamentals.definition: The degree to which a topic is relevant enough to include in reporting or decision-making.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: Whether a topic matters enough to actually report on or act on — not every possible issue deserves equal attention.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: Materiality is the filter that decides what makes it into a sustainability report at all — without it, reports would try to cover everything and say nothing.
esg-fundamentals.example: A bank's materiality assessment might rank data privacy as highly material, while land use barely registers for its own operations.
esg-fundamentals.dontConfuseWith: Double materiality — a specific two-directional version of this same idea.

esg-fundamentals.definition: Any party affected by, or able to influence, an organisation's activities.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: Anyone with a stake in what a company does — not just shareholders, but employees, customers, suppliers, communities, and regulators too.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: Almost every ESG framework is built around identifying and listening to stakeholders — it's the shift from 'who owns this company' to 'who is affected by it.'
esg-fundamentals.example: A factory's stakeholders include its workers, the town it's located in, its customers, and the river it discharges wastewater into.
esg-fundamentals.dontConfuseWith: Shareholder — a shareholder is one specific type of stakeholder (an owner); every shareholder is a stakeholder, not the reverse.

esg-fundamentals.definition: A performance framework measuring People, Planet, Profit.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: A way of judging business success on three scores at once — People, Planet, and Profit — instead of profit alone.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: It's one of the earliest and most-quoted framings of what 'sustainability' means in business, and it still shows up in mission statements today.
esg-fundamentals.example: A company reporting its triple bottom line publishes employee wellbeing metrics and carbon emissions right alongside its revenue figures.

esg-fundamentals.definition: Reporting on ESG performance alongside financial results.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: Publishing information about a company's ESG performance, not just its financial statements.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: It's the older, broader term for what the CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) now formally requires — useful for understanding why that stricter rule exists.
esg-fundamentals.example: Before CSRD made it mandatory for large EU companies, many published non-financial reporting voluntarily in a standalone sustainability report.

esg-fundamentals.definition: 17 UN development goals adopted in 2015, spanning poverty, climate, equality and more, with a 2030 target horizon — often used as a reference point for corporate impact reporting.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: 17 global goals the UN agreed on in 2015 — covering things like ending poverty, climate action, and gender equality — with a 2030 target date.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: Companies often map their own sustainability work onto specific SDGs to connect it to a globally recognized set of priorities.
esg-fundamentals.example: A renewable energy company might highlight its contribution to SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) in its annual report.

esg-fundamentals.definition: Assessing both the company's impact on people/planet and the impact of ESG factors on the company's financial value.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: You look in two directions at once: how the company affects people and the planet, and how sustainability issues could affect the company financially.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: It is the core logic behind CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) and ESRS (European Sustainability Reporting Standards) reporting — it decides which sustainability topics a company must report on.
esg-fundamentals.example: A food company affects water resources through its operations, while water scarcity can also disrupt its own production — both directions count.
esg-fundamentals.dontConfuseWith: Financial materiality — that is only the outside-in half of double materiality.

esg-fundamentals.definition: The 'inside-out' perspective of double materiality: the organisation's impact on people and the environment.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: The 'inside-out' half of double materiality: how the company's own activities affect people and the environment.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: Separating this from financial materiality is what makes double materiality genuinely 'double' rather than a rebrand of ordinary risk assessment.
esg-fundamentals.example: A mining company's impact materiality flags its effect on local biodiversity, even where that effect has no obvious impact on its own profits.
esg-fundamentals.dontConfuseWith: Financial materiality — the other, opposite-facing half of double materiality.

esg-fundamentals.definition: The 'outside-in' perspective of double materiality: how ESG factors affect the organisation's financial value.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: The 'outside-in' half of double materiality: how ESG issues out in the world could affect the company's own financial value.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: This is the half investors traditionally cared about most — it is the ESG version of ordinary financial risk.
esg-fundamentals.example: Rising carbon prices could raise costs for a manufacturer — that is a financial materiality concern, distinct from the emissions themselves.
esg-fundamentals.dontConfuseWith: Impact materiality — the other, outward-facing half of double materiality.

esg-fundamentals.definition: The view that a company's primary purpose is to maximise shareholder value.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: The traditional idea that a company exists mainly to make money for its owners, with other concerns treated as secondary.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: It is the philosophy ESG and stakeholder theory are often positioned against — worth knowing what the ESG shift is a shift away from.
esg-fundamentals.example: A CEO citing shareholder primacy might justify a decision purely by its effect on the share price, without weighing other stakeholders.
esg-fundamentals.dontConfuseWith: Stakeholder theory — its direct philosophical opposite.

esg-fundamentals.definition: R. Edward Freeman's view that companies are accountable to all stakeholders, not just shareholders.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: R. Edward Freeman's idea that a company is accountable to everyone it affects, not just the people who own its shares.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: It is the intellectual foundation behind most modern ESG and stakeholder-engagement practice.
esg-fundamentals.example: A company following stakeholder theory might delay a plant closure to give a factory town time to adjust, even if a faster closure would be cheaper.

esg-fundamentals.definition: Systematically factoring ESG issues into investment or business decisions.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: Weaving ESG factors into everyday business or investment decisions, instead of treating them as a separate side project.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: It marks the difference between a company that has a sustainability report and one that actually factors ESG into how it runs the business.
esg-fundamentals.example: A fund practicing ESG integration factors a company's carbon transition risk directly into its valuation model, not just an ethics screen.

esg-fundamentals.definition: A community's or stakeholders' implicit approval for a company to operate.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: The informal, unwritten approval a community gives a company to keep operating in its area.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: It is not a legal permit — but losing it, through protests, boycotts, or reputational damage, can shut a project down just as effectively.
esg-fundamentals.example: A mining project with every legal permit in order can still be stopped by sustained local opposition — that is a loss of social license to operate.

esg-fundamentals.definition: A fair shift to a sustainable economy in which no group bears a disproportionate burden.
esg-fundamentals.plainEnglish: Moving to a sustainable, low-carbon economy in a way that does not unfairly dump the costs on any one group — especially workers in declining industries.
esg-fundamentals.whyItMatters: Climate policy that ignores this risk creates exactly the backlash that slows climate action down — it is as much a social concept as an environmental one.
esg-fundamentals.example: A coal region investing in retraining programs for displaced miners as it shifts to renewable energy is pursuing a just transition.

csr-ethics.definition: A company's voluntary responsibility for its impact on society and the environment.
csr-ethics.plainEnglish: A company's voluntary responsibility for the impact it has on society and the environment, beyond what the law strictly requires.
csr-ethics.whyItMatters: It's the older, less rigorous cousin of ESG — understanding the difference helps you spot when a company is talking about good intentions rather than measurable performance.
csr-ethics.example: A company's CSR program might include employee volunteering days and charitable donations, alongside its formal ESG reporting.
csr-ethics.dontConfuseWith: ESG — ESG is the measurable framework investors and regulators use to assess performance; CSR is a company's voluntary program of doing good, and doesn't require the same rigor.

csr-ethics.definition: An internal document setting behavioural rules for employees and business partners.
csr-ethics.plainEnglish: An internal document laying out the behavioural rules employees and business partners are expected to follow.
csr-ethics.whyItMatters: It's the written standard that social audits actually check suppliers and staff against — without one, there's nothing concrete to audit compliance with.
csr-ethics.example: A supplier code of conduct might explicitly prohibit forced labour and set minimum safety standards for factory conditions.

csr-ethics.definition: The study of moral principles applied to business context and decision-making.
csr-ethics.plainEnglish: The study of moral principles as they apply to business decisions and conduct.
csr-ethics.whyItMatters: It covers the grey areas compliance doesn't reach — a decision can be perfectly legal and still be a business ethics failure.
csr-ethics.example: A company deciding whether to sell a product it knows is legal but potentially harmful is facing a business ethics question, not just a compliance one.
csr-ethics.dontConfuseWith: Compliance — compliance is meeting the legal minimum; business ethics asks what's right even where the law is silent.

csr-ethics.definition: Voluntary, non-core contributions a company makes to social causes.
csr-ethics.plainEnglish: Voluntary contributions a company makes to social causes that sit outside its core business — donations, sponsorships, charitable giving.
csr-ethics.whyItMatters: It's the most visible but least strategic layer of corporate social engagement — a useful contrast to concepts like shared value, which try to tie social impact directly to the business itself.
csr-ethics.example: A company donating a percentage of profits to a local charity, unrelated to its own products or operations, is practicing corporate philanthropy.
csr-ethics.dontConfuseWith: Shared value — shared value creates business value *and* social value together; philanthropy is a separate, non-core spend.

csr-ethics.definition: The risk of damage to an organisation's standing from (perceived) unethical conduct.
csr-ethics.plainEnglish: The risk that an organisation's standing gets damaged by conduct that is — or is perceived to be — unethical.
csr-ethics.whyItMatters: It's often the fastest and most direct channel through which an ESG failure (a scandal, a greenwashing claim exposed as false) turns into a financial one.
csr-ethics.example: A company caught making a false sustainability claim can suffer a stock price drop from reputational risk long before any regulator fines it.

csr-ethics.definition: Adhering to laws, regulations and internal standards.
csr-ethics.plainEnglish: Adhering to laws, regulations, and an organisation's own internal standards.
csr-ethics.whyItMatters: It's the legal floor a company has to clear — a useful baseline to contrast against business ethics, which is about doing right even beyond that floor.
csr-ethics.example: A company ensuring its factories meet all local safety regulations is achieving compliance, whether or not it goes any further.
csr-ethics.dontConfuseWith: Business ethics — compliance is about meeting the legal minimum; ethics is about what's right, which can go well beyond it.

csr-ethics.definition: A person who reports wrongdoing within an organisation, internally or externally.
csr-ethics.plainEnglish: A person who reports wrongdoing within an organisation, whether internally to management or externally to regulators or the press.
csr-ethics.whyItMatters: Whistleblowers are consistently how the most serious corporate scandals — including major ESG and greenwashing failures — actually come to light.
csr-ethics.example: An employee who reports to a regulator that their company has been falsifying emissions data is acting as a whistleblower.
csr-ethics.dontConfuseWith: Whistleblower Directive — that's the EU law protecting whistleblowers; this term is the person doing the reporting.

csr-ethics.definition: A four-layer model: economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibility.
csr-ethics.plainEnglish: A four-layer model of corporate responsibility: economic (be profitable), legal (obey the law), ethical (do what's right), and philanthropic (give back) — stacked in that order.
csr-ethics.whyItMatters: It's one of the earliest and most-taught frameworks for what a company's social responsibility actually consists of, and still shapes how CSR is discussed today.
csr-ethics.example: A business school case study explaining that a company must first be profitable and legal before its ethical and philanthropic layers can matter is applying Carroll's pyramid.

csr-ethics.definition: Porter & Kramer's strategy of creating economic value in a way that also creates societal value.
csr-ethics.plainEnglish: Michael Porter and Mark Kramer's strategy of creating economic value for the business in a way that also creates value for society, rather than treating the two as a trade-off.
csr-ethics.whyItMatters: It reframes sustainability from a cost center into a competitive strategy — an influential idea for how companies pitch their ESG efforts to investors.
csr-ethics.example: A food company investing in smallholder farmer training to secure a more reliable, higher-quality supply chain is creating shared value — better for farmers, and better for the business.
csr-ethics.dontConfuseWith: Corporate philanthropy — philanthropy is a separate, non-core spend; shared value ties the social benefit directly into how the business itself makes money.

csr-ethics.definition: The idea that companies, as 'citizens', hold rights and duties within society.
csr-ethics.plainEnglish: The idea that a company, like an individual citizen, holds both rights and responsibilities within the society it operates in.
csr-ethics.whyItMatters: It's a framing many companies use to describe their overall relationship with society — worth recognizing as closely related to, but not identical with, formal CSR or ESG programs.
csr-ethics.example: A company describing itself as 'a responsible corporate citizen' in the community where its headquarters is based is invoking this concept.

csrd-esrs.definition: The CSRD's 2014 predecessor, with lighter, less standardised requirements.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The CSRD's 2014 predecessor — an earlier EU law requiring some large companies to report non-financial information, but with much lighter, less standardised requirements.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: Knowing what came before CSRD helps explain why CSRD exists at all: NFRD's vague, inconsistent requirements are exactly what CSRD's detailed ESRS standards were built to fix.
csrd-esrs.example: Under NFRD, one company's climate disclosure might look completely different from a competitor's; CSRD's ESRS standards force them onto the same template.
csrd-esrs.dontConfuseWith: CSRD — CSRD is the newer, much stricter directive that replaced NFRD.

csrd-esrs.definition: The EU directive that mandates and standardises sustainability reporting.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The EU directive that requires large companies to report detailed, standardised, audited sustainability information — replacing the older, looser NFRD.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's the single regulation behind most of the sustainability-reporting vocabulary in this app — ESRS, double materiality, limited assurance are all CSRD machinery.
csrd-esrs.example: A large EU company preparing its first CSRD-compliant sustainability statement has to report against the detailed ESRS standards, not just write a general narrative.
csrd-esrs.dontConfuseWith: ESRS — CSRD is the law that requires reporting; ESRS are the detailed standards that specify exactly what and how to report.

csrd-esrs.definition: The mandatory, detailed reporting standards under the CSRD — a mix of cross-cutting and topic-specific standards (environment, social, governance) drafted by EFRAG.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The detailed, mandatory standards that spell out exactly what companies must report under CSRD — split into cross-cutting standards and topic-specific ones covering environment, social, and governance.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: A revised version of ESRS, cutting mandatory datapoints by roughly 61%, was adopted by the European Commission on 3 July 2026 — the standards themselves are actively being simplified, not fixed in stone.
csrd-esrs.example: A company reporting under ESRS E1 discloses its Scope 1/2/3 emissions and climate transition plan in a standardised format any reader can compare across companies.
csrd-esrs.dontConfuseWith: CSRD — ESRS are the detailed 'how to report' standards; CSRD is the law that requires reporting in the first place.

csrd-esrs.definition: The mandatory CSRD process of determining both impact and financial materiality for each ESG topic.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The mandatory CSRD process of working out, for every possible sustainability topic, both its impact materiality and its financial materiality — then reporting only on what clears the bar.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's the gatekeeping step that determines a company's entire CSRD reporting scope — get this assessment wrong and the whole report can be built on the wrong topics.
csrd-esrs.example: A logistics company's double materiality assessment might rule out biodiversity as immaterial but flag Scope 3 emissions as highly material on both dimensions.

csrd-esrs.definition: General requirements: sets out reporting principles, structure and the double materiality process.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The 'rules of the road' standard: it sets out the general reporting principles, structure, and the double materiality process every other ESRS standard builds on.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's the standard to read first — everything else in ESRS assumes you already understand the structure ESRS 1 lays out.
csrd-esrs.example: A company's reporting team reads ESRS 1 before starting to determine how the double materiality process should actually be run.

csrd-esrs.definition: General disclosures: mandatory baseline information on governance, strategy and risk management, regardless of materiality.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The baseline disclosures every company must report regardless of materiality — governance, strategy, and risk management information.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: Unlike the topic-specific standards (E1, S1, etc.), ESRS 2 can't be skipped even if a company's materiality assessment finds nothing else material.
csrd-esrs.example: Every CSRD reporter, no matter its sector, discloses its governance structure and strategy under ESRS 2.

csrd-esrs.definition: Climate change: disclosures on greenhouse gas emissions, transition plans and climate risk.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The climate change standard — covering greenhouse gas emissions, transition plans, and climate-related risk.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: For most companies this is the single most scrutinised ESRS standard, since it houses the Scope 1/2/3 emissions numbers everyone wants to compare.
csrd-esrs.example: A manufacturer's ESRS E1 disclosure includes its full Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions figures and its transition plan toward net zero.

csrd-esrs.definition: Own workforce: disclosures on working conditions, equal treatment and social dialogue.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The own-workforce standard — disclosures on working conditions, equal treatment, and social dialogue for a company's own employees.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's where mandatory metrics like the gender pay gap actually get reported under CSRD.
csrd-esrs.example: A company's ESRS S1 disclosure reports its gender pay gap and the share of its workforce covered by collective bargaining.
csrd-esrs.dontConfuseWith: ESRS S2 — S1 covers a company's own employees; S2 covers workers elsewhere in its value chain.

csrd-esrs.definition: Workers in the value chain: disclosures on working conditions at suppliers.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The value-chain workers standard — disclosures on working conditions at suppliers, not the reporting company's own staff.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It extends CSRD's social reporting beyond a company's own walls, overlapping closely with CSDDD (Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive)'s human rights due diligence obligations.
csrd-esrs.example: A retailer's ESRS S2 disclosure covers working conditions in the factories of its clothing suppliers.
csrd-esrs.dontConfuseWith: ESRS S1 — S2 covers workers in the value chain; S1 covers the company's own workforce.

csrd-esrs.definition: Business conduct: disclosures on anti-corruption, lobbying activities and supplier payment practices.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The business conduct standard — disclosures on anti-corruption, lobbying activity, and supplier payment practices.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's where governance topics like lobbying transparency and supplier payment terms formally enter CSRD reporting.
csrd-esrs.example: A company's ESRS G1 disclosure includes how quickly it pays small suppliers and what it spent on lobbying activities.

csrd-esrs.definition: The original staggered rollout: large listed companies first, then large unlisted companies, then listed SMEs (small and medium-sized enterprises). Directive 2026/470 (in force since 18 March 2026) removed listed SMEs from CSRD's mandatory scope entirely, so this original wave structure no longer reflects who has to report.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: How CSRD's staggered rollout was originally supposed to work — large listed companies first, then large unlisted, then listed SMEs (small and medium-sized enterprises). That third wave no longer applies: listed SMEs were taken out of mandatory scope altogether by the 2026 Omnibus reform.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's useful to know this history to understand how CSRD's scope evolved, but treating it as the current rollout is now inaccurate — mandatory CSRD reporting today applies only to companies exceeding both 1,000 employees and €450 million turnover, decided by that threshold rather than a wave number.
csrd-esrs.example: A large listed company was already reporting under the original CSRD wave 1 — but a listed SME that once expected to join in a later wave no longer has a mandatory CSRD obligation at all, post-Omnibus.

csrd-esrs.definition: Determines which entities (own organisation, subsidiaries, value chain) are included in reporting.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The decision about which entities — the company itself, its subsidiaries, its value chain — are actually covered by a given CSRD disclosure.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: The same topic can have a very different reporting boundary depending on the standard — getting this wrong means either under- or over-reporting.
csrd-esrs.example: A parent company's reporting boundary for its own emissions might exclude a subsidiary it doesn't have operational control over.

csrd-esrs.definition: The requirement to also report upstream (suppliers) and downstream (customers/use) ESG impacts.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The requirement to report ESG impacts not just from a company's own operations, but also upstream (its suppliers) and downstream (its customers' use of its products).
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: For most companies this is where the largest share of their real impact sits — think Scope 3 emissions — even though it's the hardest data to collect.
csrd-esrs.example: A car manufacturer's value chain reporting covers emissions from its steel suppliers upstream and from drivers using its cars downstream.

csrd-esrs.definition: A concrete action plan aligning a company's business model with a 1.5°C pathway. ESRS E1 makes disclosing this mandatory — but as a reporting requirement, not a requirement to actually have a plan: a company without one must instead disclose that fact, and state if and when it expects to adopt one.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The company doesn't have to have a transition plan under ESRS E1 — but it does have to report, either way: describe the plan if it has one, or explain that it doesn't and when (if ever) it plans to get one.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's easy to conflate 'mandatory disclosure' with 'mandatory to have' — they're not the same thing. This distinction matters even more since the 2026 Omnibus reform deleted CSDDD (Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive)'s separate requirement to actually adopt and implement such a plan; ESRS E1's reporting duty is now effectively the only requirement still standing here, and even that duty stops at disclosure, not action.
csrd-esrs.example: A company's ESRS E1 disclosure either describes specific decarbonisation milestones for 2030 and 2040 as part of its climate transition plan, or states plainly that it has no such plan yet and gives a timeline for adopting one.
csrd-esrs.dontConfuseWith: Climate transition plan (CSDDD) — that separate CSDDD obligation to adopt and implement a plan was removed by the 2026 Omnibus reform; this ESRS reporting requirement remains.

csrd-esrs.definition: European Financial Reporting Advisory Group: develops the ESRS on behalf of the European Commission.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: European Financial Reporting Advisory Group — the Brussels-based technical body that actually drafts the ESRS standards for the European Commission to formally adopt.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: When ESRS content changes — like the July 2026 simplification — EFRAG is the body that did the technical drafting behind it.
csrd-esrs.example: EFRAG published the draft revised ESRS for public consultation before the Commission formally adopted them in July 2026.

csrd-esrs.definition: Temporary reliefs (e.g. no Scope 3 in year one) easing companies into the reporting burden.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: Temporary reliefs that ease companies into CSRD reporting — for example, being allowed to skip Scope 3 emissions data in the very first reporting year.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: They soften the practical shock of a company's first CSRD report, recognising that some data — especially Scope 3 — takes time to build the systems to collect.
csrd-esrs.example: A company in its first CSRD reporting year might use a phase-in provision to report only Scope 1 and 2 emissions, adding Scope 3 the following year.

csrd-esrs.definition: Biodiversity and ecosystems: disclosures on impacts on, and dependencies on, natural capital.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The biodiversity and ecosystems standard — disclosures on how a company impacts, and depends on, natural capital.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's the standard that formally brings biodiversity loss and nature dependency into mandatory financial-grade reporting, not just voluntary environmental messaging.
csrd-esrs.example: A food company's ESRS E4 disclosure might cover its impact on soil health and its dependency on stable water availability.

csrd-esrs.definition: The three categories structuring the materiality assessment under ESRS.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The three categories — Impacts, Risks, Opportunities — that structure every materiality assessment under ESRS.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's the actual analytical lens ESRS uses to decide what's material: not just 'is this a risk,' but also 'is this an impact we cause' and 'is this an opportunity we could capture.'
csrd-esrs.example: A company's IRO analysis for water might flag drought as a risk, its own water consumption as an impact, and water-efficient product design as an opportunity.

csrd-esrs.definition: The requirement to tag CSRD disclosures in machine-readable form (XBRL — eXtensible Business Reporting Language) within the EU's single electronic reporting format (ESEF — European Single Electronic Format).
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The requirement to tag CSRD disclosures in a standardised, machine-readable format — XBRL (eXtensible Business Reporting Language) — filed in the EU's single electronic format, ESEF (European Single Electronic Format), so data can be automatically extracted and compared across companies.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's what turns thousands of CSRD reports from PDFs no one can compare into structured data investors and regulators can actually query at scale.
csrd-esrs.example: A company's digitally tagged emissions figure can be automatically pulled into a database alongside the same figure from hundreds of other companies.

csrd-esrs.definition: The current, lighter level of assurance auditors must provide on CSRD reporting.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The current, lighter level of external audit CSRD reporting must undergo — the auditor checks that nothing looks obviously wrong, short of the more rigorous 'reasonable assurance' used for financial statements.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's a deliberately lower bar than financial-statement auditing, reflecting how new and difficult ESG data collection still is — though the original CSRD roadmap expected it to eventually tighten toward reasonable assurance — the 2026 Omnibus reform removed that obligation entirely, so limited assurance is now the standing requirement indefinitely, not a transitional step.
csrd-esrs.example: An auditor providing limited assurance on a company's CSRD report checks for obvious errors and inconsistencies, without verifying every figure to the same depth as financial audits.

csrd-esrs.definition: An EU reform package, finalised in 2026, that reduced the scope and administrative burden of CSRD/CSDDD (Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive) after business-sector pushback.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: A package of EU reforms, finalised in early-to-mid 2026, that reduced the scope and administrative burden of CSRD and CSDDD after pushback from businesses.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It's not a proposal anymore — it's now finalised law: the CSDDD's EU-wide civil liability regime and mandatory transition-plan obligation were both removed, and a revised ESRS with roughly 61% fewer mandatory datapoints was adopted by the Commission on 3 July 2026, applying from financial year 2027 (with early adoption possible from 2026).
csrd-esrs.example: A company that expected to report against the original 2023 ESRS text now has far fewer mandatory datapoints to collect under the revised, post-Omnibus standards.

csrd-esrs.definition: Additional, still-in-development standards per sector (e.g. oil & gas, agriculture).
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: Additional ESRS standards tailored to individual sectors — like oil & gas or agriculture — layered on top of the general cross-cutting standards.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: They're what eventually make CSRD reporting genuinely comparable within an industry, not just across the generic baseline every company shares.
csrd-esrs.example: An oil & gas company would eventually report against both the general ESRS standards and its own sector-specific ESRS once those are finalised.

csrd-esrs.definition: A simplified reporting standard that was being developed for listed small and medium-sized enterprises — EFRAG has since concluded this project; it is not part of the current post-Omnibus framework, since listed SMEs were removed from CSRD's mandatory scope entirely. The relevant current option for smaller companies is the separate voluntary sustainability reporting standard (VSME).
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: A lighter-weight reporting standard that was once being built specifically for small, listed companies — that work has since been dropped, because listed SMEs no longer have any mandatory CSRD obligation to design a lighter standard for.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: This is a good example of how quickly this space has moved: a standard that was actively being developed became unnecessary once its target audience (listed SMEs) was removed from mandatory scope by the 2026 Omnibus reform. Smaller companies today have the option of a separate voluntary standard (VSME) instead.
csrd-esrs.example: A small listed manufacturer that once expected to eventually report under LSME now has no mandatory CSRD obligation at all, and can choose to report voluntarily under VSME if it wants to.

csrd-esrs.definition: The level (group vs. individual entity) at which CSRD reporting must be prepared.
csrd-esrs.plainEnglish: The level at which CSRD reporting has to be prepared — as one consolidated group report, or separately for individual entities.
csrd-esrs.whyItMatters: It determines whether a parent company's report can cover its subsidiaries in one document, or whether each entity needs its own.
csrd-esrs.example: A multinational group typically prepares one consolidated CSRD report at group level, rather than a separate report per subsidiary.

csddd.definition: Direct suppliers (tier-1) versus suppliers of suppliers (tier-2 and beyond) in the value chain.
csddd.plainEnglish: Tier-1 suppliers are the companies you buy directly from; tier-2 and beyond are their own suppliers, further back in the chain.
csddd.whyItMatters: Most companies have decent visibility into tier-1 suppliers but very little into tier-2+ — which is exactly where the highest-risk labour and environmental abuses tend to hide.
csddd.example: A clothing brand's tier-1 supplier might be the factory that sews the garments; its tier-2 supplier is the mill that wove the fabric.

csddd.definition: Requires companies to conduct due diligence on human rights and environmental risks across the value chain.
csddd.plainEnglish: The EU directive requiring large companies to actively check for, and address, human rights and environmental risks across their entire value chain — not just their own operations.
csddd.whyItMatters: It's the law that makes 'we didn't know what our suppliers were doing' legally insufficient — companies now have to actually go looking.
csddd.example: A retailer complying with CSDDD has to assess whether any of its suppliers use forced labour, not just certify its own factories are clean.

csddd.definition: The core duty to identify, prevent, mitigate and remediate risks.
csddd.plainEnglish: The core duty at the heart of CSDDD: identify risks, prevent them where possible, mitigate what can't be prevented, and remediate any harm that still occurs.
csddd.whyItMatters: It's a four-part cycle, not a one-time check — a company can't satisfy this obligation with a single audit and then stop paying attention.
csddd.example: A company fulfilling its due diligence obligation continuously monitors supplier risk, rather than doing one certification and considering the job done.

csddd.definition: CSDDD uses a narrower concept called the 'chain of activities': upstream (raw materials, production, supply by business partners) plus a limited slice of downstream — distribution, transport and storage carried out by business partners for or on behalf of the company. Product use and end-of-life/disposal are not covered.
csddd.plainEnglish: Upstream is broad — sourcing, production, everything that goes into making the product. Downstream is deliberately narrow — just distribution, transport and storage done by a business partner acting for the company, not the full 'rest of the product's life.'
csddd.whyItMatters: It's a common misconception that CSDDD due diligence follows a product all the way to how a customer eventually uses or disposes of it — it doesn't. Getting this scope wrong leads companies to either over- or under-estimate what they actually need visibility into.
csddd.example: A furniture company's chain of activities includes the forest its timber came from (upstream) and the logistics partner that ships and stores its furniture on the company's behalf (downstream) — but not what a customer does with the furniture after buying it, or how they dispose of it.

csddd.definition: A mandatory channel through which affected parties or their representatives can lodge a complaint.
csddd.plainEnglish: A mandatory channel that lets people affected by a company's operations — or their representatives — actually file a complaint.
csddd.whyItMatters: Without a working grievance mechanism, a company has no reliable way to even learn that harm is happening deep in its value chain.
csddd.example: A worker at a supplier factory using a grievance mechanism to report unsafe conditions, without needing to go through their direct employer first.
csddd.dontConfuseWith: Community-level grievance mechanism — that's specifically for outside communities; this broader CSDDD requirement covers value-chain workers too.

csddd.definition: Originally an obligation for large companies to adopt and put into effect a Paris-aligned transition plan — the 2026 Omnibus reform deleted this requirement from CSDDD itself. Companies with a transition plan still have to report on it under CSRD's ESRS E1, but CSDDD no longer mandates having or implementing one.
csddd.plainEnglish: Originally, an obligation for large companies to adopt and actually put into effect a plan compatible with the Paris Agreement — the 2026 Omnibus reform deleted this requirement from CSDDD entirely.
csddd.whyItMatters: It's a clean example of how fast this area of law moves: what was a hard CSDDD obligation is now gone, even though the related CSRD/ESRS E1 reporting duty survives.
csddd.example: A company no longer has to adopt a Paris-aligned transition plan under CSDDD, though it still has to report on any transition plan it does have under ESRS E1.
csddd.dontConfuseWith: Climate transition plan (ESRS E1) — the ESRS reporting requirement to disclose a transition plan, where one exists, was not removed by Omnibus.

csddd.definition: Originally a phased rollout starting with the largest companies — replaced by the 2026 Omnibus reform with a single application date (26 July 2029) for all in-scope companies at once.
csddd.plainEnglish: Originally a phased rollout hitting the largest companies first — replaced by the 2026 Omnibus reform with one single application date for all in-scope companies at once.
csddd.whyItMatters: It's a good example of the Omnibus reform's general direction: less complexity, fewer separate deadlines to track.
csddd.example: Instead of tracking which wave their company falls into, compliance teams can now plan around one fixed date: 26 July 2029.

csddd.definition: Restoring an affected person, community or the environment to a situation equivalent to (or as close as possible to) what it would have been without the harm. CSDDD makes this mandatory when the company caused or jointly caused the impact; where a business partner alone caused it, remediation by the company is voluntary, alongside using its influence to get the partner to act.
csddd.plainEnglish: Actually repairing or compensating for harm — mandatory if the company itself caused or helped cause it, only voluntary (a 'should,' not a 'must') if a business partner caused the harm entirely on its own.
csddd.whyItMatters: This caused / jointly caused / solely-by-a-partner distinction is the actual legal trigger for whether remediation is mandatory — treating it as a blanket duty regardless of who caused what overstates the law.
csddd.example: A company whose own factory underpaid workers must ensure back pay is actually issued. If an independent supplier alone underpaid its workers, the company isn't legally required to remediate directly, though it's expected to use its leverage to push the supplier to fix it.

csddd.definition: The authority each member state must designate to oversee compliance and impose fines.
csddd.plainEnglish: The authority each EU member state has to designate to oversee CSDDD compliance and impose fines for breaches.
csddd.whyItMatters: Since the EU-wide civil liability regime was removed by the Omnibus reform, this national-level enforcement is now doing more of the practical work of holding companies accountable.
csddd.example: A company under investigation for a CSDDD breach would face its own member state's national supervisory authority, not a single EU-wide regulator.

csddd.definition: Originally a CSDDD provision letting victims sue a company directly under an EU-wide liability regime — removed by the 2026 Omnibus reform. Liability for CSDDD breaches is now governed by each member state's own national rules, not a harmonised EU standard.
csddd.plainEnglish: Originally, a CSDDD provision letting victims sue a company directly under a single, harmonised EU-wide liability regime — removed by the 2026 Omnibus reform.
csddd.whyItMatters: Liability for CSDDD breaches is now governed by each member state's own national rules and court procedures, not one common EU standard — meaning the practical consequences of a breach can now differ significantly by country.
csddd.example: A worker seeking compensation for harm caused by a CSDDD breach today has to rely on their own country's national liability rules, rather than a uniform EU right.

csddd.definition: The requirement to address the most severe and likely risks first when resources are limited.
csddd.plainEnglish: The requirement to tackle the most severe and most likely risks first, since no company has the resources to address everything in its value chain at once.
csddd.whyItMatters: It's what makes CSDDD compliance realistic rather than impossible — companies aren't expected to fix every risk everywhere simultaneously, just to be strategic about sequencing.
csddd.example: A company might prioritise addressing forced-labour risk at a high-risk supplier before tackling a lower-severity packaging-waste issue elsewhere.

csddd.definition: The practice of a company passing due diligence requirements down to its direct suppliers by contract.
csddd.plainEnglish: The practice of a company passing its due diligence requirements down the chain to its direct suppliers, by writing them into contracts.
csddd.whyItMatters: It's the main mechanism companies actually use to extend due diligence beyond what they can directly monitor — pushing the obligation contractually to whoever they can reach.
csddd.example: A brand's supplier contract might require the supplier to itself conduct due diligence on its own sub-suppliers, cascading the obligation further down the chain.

csddd.term: OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct
csddd.definition: The voluntary reference framework underlying the CSDDD's due diligence obligations.
csddd.plainEnglish: A voluntary reference framework for responsible business conduct that CSDDD's own due diligence obligations were built on top of.
csddd.whyItMatters: It's one of the two foundational frameworks (alongside the UNGPs) that gives CSDDD's structure its shape — worth knowing to understand where the directive's ideas actually came from.
csddd.example: A company designing its CSDDD due diligence process might use the OECD Guidelines' existing due diligence steps as a starting template.

csddd.definition: The 2011 UN framework introducing the 'protect, respect, remedy' structure, the basis for CSDDD.
csddd.plainEnglish: The 2011 UN framework that introduced the 'protect, respect, remedy' structure for business and human rights — the conceptual basis CSDDD was built on.
csddd.whyItMatters: The 'protect, respect, remedy' logic — governments protect, companies respect, victims get remedy — is the underlying architecture behind most modern supply-chain human rights law, including CSDDD.
csddd.example: CSDDD's remediation requirement traces directly back to the 'remedy' pillar of the UNGPs' original 2011 framework.

sfdr.definition: Requires financial market participants to disclose sustainability risks and impacts.
sfdr.plainEnglish: The EU regulation requiring financial market participants to disclose the sustainability risks and impacts of their products.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It's the regulation that turns vague marketing claims like 'sustainable fund' into something with actual disclosure requirements behind it.
sfdr.example: An asset manager marketing a fund as sustainable has to back that claim with SFDR-mandated pre-contractual and periodic disclosures.

sfdr.definition: SFDR term for the entities covered by the regulation: asset managers, insurers, pension funds and similar.
sfdr.plainEnglish: SFDR's term for the entities the regulation actually covers — asset managers, insurers, pension funds, and similar financial institutions.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It defines exactly who has to comply with SFDR — a useful check when figuring out whether a given financial institution is even in scope.
sfdr.example: An asset management firm managing mutual funds is a financial market participant under SFDR; a company simply issuing its own shares is not.

sfdr.definition: The process by which a fund manager determines whether a product falls under Article 6, 8 or 9.
sfdr.plainEnglish: The process a fund manager goes through to decide whether a financial product falls under Article 6, 8, or 9.
sfdr.whyItMatters: Getting this classification wrong — claiming Article 9 without earning it — is precisely the kind of greenwashing risk that draws regulatory scrutiny in the financial sector.
sfdr.example: A fund manager launching a new fund runs it through SFDR product classification before deciding whether to market it as Article 8 or Article 9.

sfdr.definition: SFDR category for financial products without a specific sustainability claim.
sfdr.plainEnglish: The SFDR category for financial products that make no specific sustainability claim at all.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It's the baseline every other SFDR category is defined against — knowing it exists helps you read a fund's classification as a real signal, not just paperwork.
sfdr.example: A conventional equity fund with no ESG angle would be classified as an Article 6 product under SFDR.
sfdr.dontConfuseWith: Article 8 and Article 9 products — those actively promote or target sustainability; Article 6 products make no such claim.

sfdr.definition: SFDR category for products promoting environmental or social characteristics ('light green').
sfdr.plainEnglish: The SFDR category — often called 'light green' — for products that promote environmental or social characteristics, without sustainable investment as their explicit core objective.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It's the most common sustainability-labelled category in practice, sitting between no claim at all (Article 6) and a full sustainable-investment objective (Article 9).
sfdr.example: A fund that screens out the worst ESG performers but doesn't require every holding to have a positive sustainability impact would typically be Article 8.
sfdr.dontConfuseWith: Article 9 — Article 9 requires sustainable investment as an explicit objective; Article 8 only requires promoting ESG characteristics.

sfdr.definition: SFDR category for products with sustainable investment as an explicit objective ('dark green').
sfdr.plainEnglish: The SFDR category — often called 'dark green' — for products that have sustainable investment as their explicit, stated objective.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It's the strictest SFDR category, and the one that has drawn the most scrutiny over whether products actually live up to the label.
sfdr.example: A fund that only invests in companies contributing measurably to renewable energy would aim to qualify as Article 9.
sfdr.dontConfuseWith: Article 8 — Article 8 only promotes ESG characteristics; Article 9 makes sustainable investment the explicit objective itself.

sfdr.definition: An investment contributing to an environmental or social objective, doing no significant harm to any other objective, and following good governance.
sfdr.plainEnglish: Under SFDR's specific definition: an investment that contributes to an environmental or social objective, does no significant harm to any other objective, and follows good governance practices.
sfdr.whyItMatters: This precise three-part test is what an Article 9 product's holdings actually have to meet — it's a much narrower bar than just being 'ESG-friendly.'
sfdr.example: A renewable energy company might qualify as a sustainable investment, but only if it also meets governance standards and doesn't cause serious harm elsewhere, like poor labour practices.
sfdr.dontConfuseWith: DNSH — the 'do no significant harm' part of this definition is directly borrowed from the EU Taxonomy's own DNSH concept.

sfdr.definition: The risk that an Article 8/9 product is presented as more sustainable than its underlying holdings justify.
sfdr.plainEnglish: The risk that an Article 8 or 9 product is marketed as more sustainable than its actual underlying holdings justify.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It's one of the main reasons regulators pushed for the SFDR 2.0 reform — the current Article 8/9 split has proven genuinely confusing for investors to judge.
sfdr.example: A fund labelled Article 8 that still holds a meaningful stake in coal companies would raise greenwashing risk concerns.

sfdr.definition: Mandatory SFDR information that must be given to investors before purchasing a financial product.
sfdr.plainEnglish: Mandatory information a fund has to give investors before they buy in — explaining exactly what sustainability claim, if any, the product is making.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It's meant to stop an investor from discovering after the fact that a 'sustainable' fund wasn't what they thought.
sfdr.example: Before buying into an Article 8 fund, an investor receives a pre-contractual disclosure explaining which environmental or social characteristics it promotes.

sfdr.definition: An annual mandatory update on the actual sustainability performance of an Article 8 or 9 product.
sfdr.plainEnglish: An annual mandatory update on how an Article 8 or 9 product actually performed against its sustainability claims.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It's the accountability check that follows the initial pre-contractual promise — a way to verify the fund kept doing what it said it would.
sfdr.example: An Article 9 fund's periodic report might show the actual share of its holdings that met its sustainable investment criteria that year.

sfdr.definition: A mandatory set of indicators measuring the main negative effects of investments on sustainability.
sfdr.plainEnglish: A mandatory set of indicators measuring the main negative effects an investment has on sustainability factors — emissions, biodiversity, social issues, and more.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It's the mechanism that forces a sustainability-labelled fund to also disclose its downsides, not just its positive story.
sfdr.example: A fund's PAI disclosure might report the carbon footprint of its portfolio companies, even if the fund's main pitch is about positive impact elsewhere.

sfdr.definition: The share of a portfolio meeting EU Taxonomy criteria, mandatory to disclose under SFDR.
sfdr.plainEnglish: The share of a fund's portfolio that meets EU Taxonomy criteria — a mandatory figure SFDR requires funds to disclose.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It connects SFDR directly to the EU Taxonomy — a fund can claim to be green in its marketing, but this number is the concrete, checkable figure behind that claim.
sfdr.example: An Article 9 fund might disclose a 65% taxonomy alignment percentage, meaning two-thirds of its portfolio meets the EU Taxonomy's strict criteria.

sfdr.definition: The requirement for the financial institution itself (not just per product) to disclose sustainability policy.
sfdr.plainEnglish: The requirement for a financial institution itself — not just each individual product it offers — to disclose its overall sustainability policy.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It means a fund manager can't hide a weak sustainability approach behind one strong-looking flagship product — the whole firm has to disclose its policy.
sfdr.example: An asset manager's entity-level disclosure describes how it integrates sustainability risk across its business, separate from any single fund's own disclosure.

sfdr.definition: Detailed technical rules ('Level 2') supplementing the main SFDR regulation.
sfdr.plainEnglish: Detailed technical rules — often called 'Level 2' — that fill in the practical specifics underneath SFDR's main, higher-level regulation.
sfdr.whyItMatters: The main SFDR text sets the principles; the RTS is where the actual reporting templates and calculation methods live.
sfdr.example: A fund manager figuring out exactly how to calculate a PAI indicator would consult the RTS, not just the main SFDR regulation.

sfdr.definition: The joint body of EBA, ESMA and EIOPA that drafts SFDR technical standards.
sfdr.plainEnglish: The joint body of the EBA, ESMA, and EIOPA — the EU's three financial-sector supervisors — that drafts SFDR's technical standards together.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It's why SFDR's detailed rules read as unified across banking, securities, and insurance/pensions — one joint body drafts the technical standards for all three.
sfdr.example: When SFDR's RTS needed updating, it was the ESAs working jointly, not any single regulator acting alone.

sfdr.definition: A November 2025 EU proposal (SFDR 2.0) to replace the Article 8/9 split with three new categories (Sustainable, Transition, ESG Basics) after criticism that the current split confuses investors — still in the legislative process as of mid-2026, with application not expected before 2028.
sfdr.plainEnglish: An EU proposal — published by the Commission in November 2025 — to replace the current Article 8/9 split with three new categories: Sustainable, Transition, and ESG Basics.
sfdr.whyItMatters: It's a direct response to years of criticism that the Article 8/9 split confuses investors — but as of mid-2026 it's still working through the EU legislative process, with application not expected before 2028, so the current Article 6/8/9 framework remains fully in force.
sfdr.example: A fund manager today still classifies products under Article 6, 8, or 9 — the proposed Sustainable/Transition/ESG Basics categories aren't in force yet.

eu-taxonomy.definition: A classification system defining which economic activities qualify as 'environmentally sustainable'.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: A classification system that defines, activity by activity, which economic activities actually qualify as 'environmentally sustainable' under EU rules.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: It's the reference standard other frameworks build on — SFDR's taxonomy alignment percentage and the EU Green Bond Standard both depend directly on it.
eu-taxonomy.example: A solar power project might qualify under the EU Taxonomy as an environmentally sustainable activity, while a coal plant would not.

eu-taxonomy.definition: Climate mitigation, climate adaptation, water, circular economy, pollution, biodiversity.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: The six goals the EU Taxonomy is built around: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, water, circular economy, pollution prevention, and biodiversity.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: Every activity has to be checked against all six — contributing substantially to one is not enough if it seriously harms any of the other five.
eu-taxonomy.example: A hydropower project might substantially contribute to climate mitigation, but still needs to pass a 'do no significant harm' check against water and biodiversity.

eu-taxonomy.definition: The requirement that an activity contributes materially to at least one of the six environmental objectives.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: The requirement that an activity contributes materially — not just marginally — to at least one of the Taxonomy's six environmental objectives.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: It's the first of two hurdles (alongside DNSH) an activity has to clear to be Taxonomy-aligned — a token or marginal benefit isn't enough.
eu-taxonomy.example: A building renovation that cuts energy use by a meaningful, specified percentage could count as a substantial contribution to climate mitigation.

eu-taxonomy.definition: The requirement that an activity does not significantly harm any of the other five objectives.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: The requirement that, while contributing to one environmental objective, an activity doesn't seriously damage any of the other five.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: It's what stops an activity from being labelled sustainable purely on one dimension while quietly causing serious harm elsewhere.
eu-taxonomy.example: A biofuel project might substantially contribute to climate mitigation but fail DNSH if it causes serious biodiversity loss through land clearing.
eu-taxonomy.dontConfuseWith: Substantial contribution — that's the positive requirement; DNSH is the separate negative check against the other five objectives.

eu-taxonomy.definition: An activity included in the taxonomy, regardless of whether it actually meets the criteria.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: An activity that's included in the Taxonomy's list at all — regardless of whether it actually meets the detailed criteria to be considered sustainable.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: Eligible is a much weaker claim than aligned — a lot of reporting confusion comes from blurring the two together.
eu-taxonomy.example: Cement production is a taxonomy-eligible activity, since it's on the list, even though most cement production doesn't yet meet the strict alignment criteria.
eu-taxonomy.dontConfuseWith: Taxonomy-aligned activity — eligibility just means the activity is covered by the Taxonomy at all; alignment means it actually meets every criterion.

eu-taxonomy.definition: An activity that is both eligible and actually meets all criteria (substantial contribution + DNSH + safeguards).
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: An activity that's both eligible and actually meets every criterion required: substantial contribution, DNSH, and the minimum safeguards.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: This is the number that actually matters in taxonomy alignment percentage disclosures — being merely eligible doesn't count toward it.
eu-taxonomy.example: A wind farm that meets all the specific technical screening criteria for climate mitigation would count as taxonomy-aligned, not just eligible.
eu-taxonomy.dontConfuseWith: Taxonomy-eligible activity — eligibility is just being on the list; alignment means passing every actual test.

eu-taxonomy.definition: The requirement that an activity meets baseline social safeguards (OECD Guidelines, UNGPs).
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: A baseline requirement that a taxonomy-aligned activity also meets basic social standards, referencing the OECD Guidelines and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs).
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: It stops an activity from qualifying as 'environmentally sustainable' while still being built on serious labour or human rights abuses.
eu-taxonomy.example: A mining project that's environmentally sound but relies on forced labour would fail the minimum safeguards test, even with a strong environmental profile.

eu-taxonomy.definition: Detailed, activity-specific thresholds determining whether substantial contribution and DNSH are met.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: Detailed, activity-specific thresholds that spell out exactly what counts as substantial contribution and DNSH for a given activity.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: They're what turns the Taxonomy's six broad objectives into concrete, checkable numbers a company can actually test its activities against.
eu-taxonomy.example: For a building, the technical screening criteria might specify a maximum energy-use threshold that has to be met to count as substantially contributing to climate mitigation.

eu-taxonomy.definition: The three financial metrics companies use to report taxonomy alignment — turnover, CapEx and OpEx. A 2026 Omnibus-driven simplification (the revised Delegated Act, in force since 28 January 2026) added a 10% materiality threshold: activities that cumulatively fall below it can be excluded from assessment, and non-financial companies can omit the OpEx KPI entirely if it isn't material to their business.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: The three financial metrics — capital expenditure, operating expenditure, and turnover — that companies must use to report how much of their business is taxonomy-aligned. Since a 2026 simplification, small or immaterial activities (below a 10% threshold) no longer need to be individually assessed.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: It turns taxonomy alignment from a yes/no label into a graduated percentage a company reports across three different angles of its finances — though the 2026 reform cut the actual reporting burden substantially (roughly 64% fewer required datapoints for non-financial companies), precisely by letting companies skip assessing activities that don't meaningfully move the needle.
eu-taxonomy.example: A company might report that 20% of its turnover but 45% of its CapEx is taxonomy-aligned, reflecting new green investment ahead of current revenue — and, under the simplified 2026 rules, can skip assessing a minor product line worth only 3% of turnover, since it falls under the 10% materiality threshold.

eu-taxonomy.definition: An activity with no low-carbon alternative that qualifies temporarily as sustainable while meeting the sector's best-performing level.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: An activity with no low-carbon alternative yet available, that temporarily qualifies as taxonomy-aligned if it performs at the best level currently achievable in its sector.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: It's the Taxonomy's acknowledgment that some sectors can't leap straight to zero-carbon — a pragmatic bridge, not a permanent exemption.
eu-taxonomy.example: A cement plant using the most efficient currently available production process might qualify as a transitional activity, pending genuinely low-carbon cement technology.

eu-taxonomy.definition: An activity that doesn't itself meet an environmental objective but enables other activities to contribute substantially.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: An activity that doesn't itself meet an environmental objective, but makes it possible for other activities to substantially contribute to one.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: It recognises that some genuinely essential green infrastructure — like grid upgrades — doesn't reduce emissions directly itself, but is what allows other activities to.
eu-taxonomy.example: Manufacturing components for wind turbines is an enabling activity — it doesn't generate renewable energy itself, but makes wind power generation possible.

eu-taxonomy.definition: Supplementary EU legislation setting out the technical screening criteria per sector.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: Supplementary EU legislation that sets out the detailed technical screening criteria for each sector under the Taxonomy.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: The main Taxonomy Regulation sets the framework; delegated acts are where the actual sector-by-sector detail gets filled in and updated over time.
eu-taxonomy.example: A new delegated act might add specific technical screening criteria for a sector the Taxonomy hadn't yet detailed.

eu-taxonomy.definition: A mandatory indicator for banks measuring the share of taxonomy-aligned assets on the balance sheet.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: A mandatory indicator for banks measuring what share of their overall balance sheet is made up of taxonomy-aligned assets.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: It's the banking sector's own version of a taxonomy alignment percentage — a way to judge how green a bank's actual lending book is, not just its marketing.
eu-taxonomy.example: A bank might disclose a Green Asset Ratio of 8%, showing that only a small share of its total lending currently meets taxonomy-aligned criteria.

eu-taxonomy.definition: Sectors at heightened risk of production relocation, subject to stricter or different criteria.
eu-taxonomy.plainEnglish: Sectors judged to be at heightened risk of relocating production to avoid EU climate rules, and which the Taxonomy subjects to stricter or different criteria as a result.
eu-taxonomy.whyItMatters: It's the Taxonomy's own version of the same carbon leakage concern behind the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) — recognising that stringent rules can backfire if companies simply move abroad.
eu-taxonomy.example: A heavy industry sector flagged as carbon leakage risk might face different technical screening criteria than a sector with no realistic option to relocate.

gri-standards.definition: The oldest and most widely used global sustainability reporting standard.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: The oldest and most widely used global sustainability reporting standard, used voluntarily by companies worldwide long before CSRD made reporting mandatory in the EU.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: It's the reference point ESRS itself was built with an eye toward — many companies reporting under GRI for years now also have to add CSRD/ESRS on top.
gri-standards.example: A company outside the EU with no CSRD obligation might still publish a voluntary GRI report to meet investor expectations.
gri-standards.dontConfuseWith: ESRS — GRI is a voluntary global standard; ESRS is the EU's own mandatory standard, though the two are working toward interoperability.

gri-standards.definition: A mandatory overview linking each reported indicator to its exact location in the report.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: A mandatory table linking every indicator a GRI report claims to cover to its exact location in the document.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: Without it, a reader would have to hunt through a long report to check whether a specific disclosure was actually made — the index makes every claim verifiable.
gri-standards.example: A GRI content index might show that GRI 305 (Emissions) data appears on page 42 of the sustainability report.

gri-standards.definition: A GRI report can stand alone or form part of a broader integrated annual report.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: A GRI report can either stand alone as its own document, or be woven into a broader integrated annual report alongside financial results.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: It affects how a reader finds sustainability information — buried in one combined annual report, or published as its own separate document.
gri-standards.example: A company might publish a single integrated report combining financial results and its GRI-based sustainability disclosures in one document.

gri-standards.definition: The three baseline standards (GRI 1, 2, 3) that apply to every reporting organisation.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: The three baseline standards — GRI 1, 2, and 3 — that every organisation reporting under GRI has to apply, regardless of sector.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: They're the mandatory floor beneath GRI reporting, similar in role to ESRS 1 and 2 under CSRD.
gri-standards.example: Every GRI reporter, from a bank to a mining company, applies the same GRI Universal Standards before adding any topic-specific disclosures.

gri-standards.definition: Sets out the reporting principles and baseline requirements every GRI report must meet.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: The GRI standard setting out the basic reporting principles and requirements every GRI report has to meet.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: It's the starting point for understanding how to use GRI at all — much like ESRS 1 is for CSRD.
gri-standards.example: A company's reporting team consults GRI 1 to understand the core principles before applying any topic-specific standard.

gri-standards.definition: Requires baseline information on the organisation, governance and stakeholder engagement.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: The GRI standard requiring baseline information about the organisation itself — its structure, governance, and how it engages with stakeholders.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: It's the context every reader needs before interpreting a company's specific sustainability topics — who is this company, and how is it governed.
gri-standards.example: A company's GRI 2 disclosure describes its ownership structure, its board, and how it consulted stakeholders in preparing the report.

gri-standards.definition: Describes the process for identifying and reporting on material topics.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: The GRI standard describing the process for identifying which sustainability topics are actually material enough to report on.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: It's GRI's own version of a materiality process — worth comparing to ESRS's double materiality assessment, since the two aren't identical.
gri-standards.example: A company follows GRI 3's process to determine that water use is material for its operations, while employee volunteering isn't.
gri-standards.dontConfuseWith: Materiality assessment (GRI) — GRI 3 is the standard describing the process; the materiality assessment is that process actually being carried out.

gri-standards.definition: Topic-specific standards (e.g. GRI 305 Emissions, GRI 408 Child Labor) prescribing concrete indicators.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: Topic-specific GRI standards — like GRI 305 on Emissions or GRI 408 on Child Labor — that prescribe concrete indicators once a topic is found material.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: These are where the actual, comparable numbers come from — the Universal Standards set the rules, but Topic Standards are what get reported.
gri-standards.example: A company that finds emissions material under GRI 3 then reports specific figures required by GRI 305, the Topic Standard for Emissions.

gri-standards.definition: The GRI 3 process where impact on the economy, environment and people is central, not necessarily financial materiality.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: The GRI 3 process of identifying material topics, centred on the organisation's impact on the economy, environment, and people — not primarily on financial materiality.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: It's a meaningfully different lens than ESRS's double materiality: GRI's traditional focus is impact-first, closer to only one half of the ESRS approach.
gri-standards.example: A GRI materiality assessment might flag a company's water pollution as material because of its impact on local communities, independent of any financial cost to the company.
gri-standards.dontConfuseWith: Double materiality assessment (ESRS) — ESRS explicitly requires both impact and financial materiality; GRI's traditional approach centres on impact.

gri-standards.definition: Sector-specific standards (e.g. oil & gas, mining, agriculture) prescribing the key material topics per sector.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: Sector-specific GRI standards — for oil & gas, mining, agriculture, and others — that prescribe the key material topics typical of that sector.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: They save every company in a sector from independently reinventing which topics matter most for their industry.
gri-standards.example: A mining company uses the GRI Sector Standard for mining to identify tailings management as a likely material topic, before running its own assessment.

gri-standards.definition: The independent standard-setting body, operationally separate from the rest of GRI, that sets and maintains the GRI Standards.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: The independent standard-setting body, operationally separate from the rest of GRI, that actually writes and maintains the GRI Standards.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: Its independence from GRI's other operations is what gives the standards their credibility as a technical, not commercial, product.
gri-standards.example: When GRI Universal Standards were revised in 2021, it was the GSSB that carried out the technical drafting.

gri-standards.definition: A formal claim that a report meets all Universal Standards requirements.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: A formal claim a company can make that its report meets every requirement of the GRI Universal Standards, not just references GRI loosely.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: It's a meaningful quality signal — a report can mention GRI without earning the right to claim it's 'in accordance with' it.
gri-standards.example: A company claiming to report 'in accordance with GRI' has to be able to demonstrate every Universal Standards requirement was actually met.

gri-standards.definition: Cooperation between GRI and EFRAG to minimise overlap between GRI indicators and ESRS requirements.
gri-standards.plainEnglish: Ongoing cooperation between GRI and EFRAG (European Financial Reporting Advisory Group) to reduce duplication between GRI indicators and ESRS requirements.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: Without it, a company already reporting under GRI would have to redo much of the same work from scratch for CSRD — this work is what lets some of it be reused.
gri-standards.example: A company might satisfy part of its ESRS S1 workforce disclosure with data it already collects for its existing GRI report, thanks to interoperability mapping.

gri-standards.definition: Determining where a reporting obligation for an indicator begins and ends (own operations vs. value chain).
gri-standards.plainEnglish: Determining where a GRI reporting obligation for a given indicator actually begins and ends — a company's own operations, or its value chain too.
gri-standards.whyItMatters: It's GRI's version of the same boundary question ESRS asks — get it wrong and a report either misses real impacts or takes on more than it can substantiate.
gri-standards.example: A company might set the boundary for its emissions reporting to include Scope 3 supplier emissions, but limit its labour-practices reporting to its own direct employees.

other-reporting-standards.definition: A non-profit platform where companies and cities voluntarily disclose environmental data and receive a letter score.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: A non-profit platform where companies and cities voluntarily disclose environmental data — climate, water, forests — and receive a letter grade score.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: Large customers often require their suppliers to fill out CDP questionnaires, making it a de facto reporting requirement even without any law behind it.
other-reporting-standards.example: A supplier might be required by a major retail customer to submit a CDP Climate Change questionnaire response every year, regardless of any regulatory obligation.

other-reporting-standards.definition: The most widely used voluntary climate-data reporting form, often required by large customers in the value chain.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: The most widely used voluntary form for reporting climate data — often the specific document large customers demand from suppliers in their value chain.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It's a concrete, standardised document a company can actually be asked to fill in, unlike vaguer expectations to 'report on climate.'
other-reporting-standards.example: A manufacturer completing its CDP Climate Change questionnaire reports its Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions in CDP's standard format.

other-reporting-standards.definition: An external party (auditor or specialised firm) verifying the reliability of reported data.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: An external party — an auditor or a specialised firm — that independently verifies how reliable a company's reported sustainability data actually is.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It's what separates a genuinely audited disclosure from a company simply asserting its own numbers are correct.
other-reporting-standards.example: An accounting firm acting as the assurance provider for a company's CSRD report checks the underlying data before signing off with limited assurance.

other-reporting-standards.definition: Sector-specific, investor-focused standards, now under the ISSB (International Sustainability Standards Board) since 2022.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: Sector-specific, investor-focused reporting standards — now absorbed into the ISSB (International Sustainability Standards Board) since 2022.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It represents the financial-materiality-only, investor-first approach to ESG reporting — a useful contrast to GRI and ESRS's broader, double-materiality view.
other-reporting-standards.example: An investor comparing two oil companies' financial exposure to climate risk might look at their SASB-aligned disclosures rather than a broader GRI report.
