other-reporting-standards.dontConfuseWith: Double vs. single materiality (standards) — SASB applies primarily financial (single) materiality, unlike GRI/ESRS's double materiality.

other-reporting-standards.term: TCFD (Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures)
other-reporting-standards.definition: A voluntary framework, published in 2017, for disclosing climate-related financial risk across four pillars: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics/targets.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: A voluntary framework, published in 2017, for disclosing climate-related financial risk across four pillars: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics & targets.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: Its four-pillar structure became so influential that it was carried almost directly into IFRS S2 and TNFD — understanding TCFD explains the shape of both.
other-reporting-standards.example: A bank's climate risk disclosure organised under governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics is following the TCFD structure, whether or not it says so explicitly.

other-reporting-standards.definition: General requirements for disclosure of sustainability-related financial information, issued by the ISSB under the IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) Foundation.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: The ISSB's general standard — issued under the IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) Foundation — for disclosing sustainability-related financial information; the baseline companion to IFRS S2's specific climate focus.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It's the ISSB's global-baseline answer to ESRS 1 and 2 — investor-focused, financial-materiality-only, and designed for comparability across markets worldwide.
other-reporting-standards.example: A company reporting under IFRS S1 discloses the governance and strategy behind all of its material sustainability risks, not just climate.
other-reporting-standards.dontConfuseWith: IFRS S2 — S1 is the general baseline standard; S2 is specifically about climate.

other-reporting-standards.definition: Climate-related disclosures, built directly on the TCFD structure.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: The ISSB's climate-specific disclosure standard, built directly on TCFD's four-pillar structure.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It's effectively TCFD formalised into a global reporting standard — if you understand TCFD's four pillars, you already understand IFRS S2's backbone.
other-reporting-standards.example: A company's IFRS S2 disclosure covers its climate governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics & targets, following the same structure TCFD established.
other-reporting-standards.dontConfuseWith: IFRS S1 — S2 is climate-specific; S1 is the general baseline standard covering all sustainability topics.

other-reporting-standards.definition: Governance, strategy, risk management, metrics & targets: a structure echoed in TNFD and IFRS S2.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: Governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics & targets — the four-part structure TCFD introduced for climate disclosure.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: This exact structure was echoed almost unchanged in both TNFD and IFRS S2, making it worth memorising once rather than three separate times.
other-reporting-standards.example: A company's climate report organised into these four sections is following the same skeleton used across TCFD, TNFD, and IFRS S2.

other-reporting-standards.definition: The distinction between broad standards (GRI Universal, ESRS 2) and standards tailored to one sector (SASB, GRI Sector Standards).
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: The distinction between broad standards that apply to every company (like GRI Universal Standards or ESRS 2) and standards tailored to one specific sector (like SASB or GRI Sector Standards).
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It explains why a company might need to consult two different types of standard at once — one for the baseline, one for what's specific to its industry.
other-reporting-standards.example: An oil company applies a sector-agnostic governance disclosure alongside a sector-specific standard covering methane leakage, unique to its industry.

other-reporting-standards.definition: A framework, launched in 2023 and modeled on TCFD's four-pillar structure, for disclosing nature and biodiversity-related financial risk.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: A framework, launched in 2023 and modeled directly on TCFD's four-pillar structure, for disclosing nature and biodiversity-related financial risk.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It does for biodiversity loss and nature dependency what TCFD did for climate — turning a previously vague environmental concern into a structured financial disclosure.
other-reporting-standards.example: A food company using TNFD's structure might disclose its financial exposure to water scarcity risk in the same governance/strategy/risk/metrics format TCFD popularised.

other-reporting-standards.definition: A framework (formerly run by the IIRC — International Integrated Reporting Council — now under the IFRS Foundation) combining financial and non-financial value creation into one narrative via six capitals.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: A framework — originally built by the IIRC (International Integrated Reporting Council), now under the IFRS Foundation — that combines financial and non-financial value creation into one single narrative report, built around six capitals.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It's a genuinely different philosophy from GRI/ESRS/SASB — instead of separate sustainability sections, it tries to tell one integrated story of how a company creates value.
other-reporting-standards.example: A company following <IR> might structure its entire annual report around how it uses and builds each of the six capitals, rather than having a separate sustainability chapter.

other-reporting-standards.definition: Financial, manufactured, intellectual, human, social/relationship and natural capital.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: The six resources Integrated Reporting says a company draws on and builds: financial, manufactured, intellectual, human, social/relationship, and natural capital.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It's a deliberately broader lens than 'ESG' — explicitly including things like brand reputation (intellectual) and employee skills (human) as capitals a company manages.
other-reporting-standards.example: A company's <IR> report might describe how an investment in employee training builds human capital, alongside a factory upgrade that builds manufactured capital.

other-reporting-standards.definition: A former framework for climate and environmental reporting, folded into the ISSB in 2022.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: A former framework for climate and environmental reporting that was folded into the ISSB in 2022.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It's one of several once-separate standard-setters (alongside SASB and the IIRC) that have since consolidated into the ISSB — useful context for why the standards landscape looks less fragmented than it used to.
other-reporting-standards.example: A company that once reported under CDSB guidance would now find that content absorbed into the ISSB's IFRS S1/S2 standards instead.

other-reporting-standards.definition: The 2021 merger of SASB and the IIRC, itself later absorbed into the ISSB.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: The organisation formed by the 2021 merger of SASB and the IIRC (which ran Integrated Reporting) — itself later absorbed into the ISSB.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It marks a key step in the broader trend of sustainability standard-setters consolidating rather than multiplying.
other-reporting-standards.example: A reporting professional researching SASB's history would find it passed through the Value Reporting Foundation before ending up under the ISSB.

other-reporting-standards.definition: A method for stress-testing a strategy against different climate pathways (e.g. 1.5C vs. 4C scenarios).
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: A method for stress-testing a company's strategy against different possible climate futures — for example, a 1.5°C pathway versus a 4°C pathway.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It forces a company to show its strategy would actually survive a range of climate outcomes, not just the one it's hoping for.
other-reporting-standards.example: An insurer's scenario analysis might show how its claims exposure changes under a 1.5°C scenario versus a 4°C scenario with much more severe extreme weather.

other-reporting-standards.definition: Locate, Evaluate, Assess, Prepare: the process companies use to map nature-related risks.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: Locate, Evaluate, Assess, Prepare — the four-step process TNFD recommends companies use to map their nature-related risks.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It's TNFD's practical starting point — a company that doesn't know where to begin with nature risk can follow LEAP as a structured first pass.
other-reporting-standards.example: A company starting its TNFD journey might use the 'Locate' step to identify which of its sites sit in water-stressed regions.

other-reporting-standards.definition: ESRS/GRI apply double materiality; SASB/IFRS S1&S2 apply primarily financial (single) materiality.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: A key dividing line between reporting standards: ESRS and GRI apply double materiality (impact and financial); SASB and IFRS S1/S2 apply primarily financial (single) materiality.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It explains why the same company can produce a materiality assessment for ESRS that looks quite different from one built for SASB or IFRS S1/S2 — they're answering a different question.
other-reporting-standards.example: A company's SASB report might exclude a topic as immaterial financially, even though the same topic would be flagged as material under ESRS's impact lens.

other-reporting-standards.definition: Standard scenarios from the Network for Greening the Financial System, widely used in TCFD/IFRS S2 scenario analysis.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: A standard set of climate scenarios published by the Network for Greening the Financial System, widely used as the reference scenarios in TCFD and IFRS S2 scenario analysis.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: Using a shared, credible set of scenarios (rather than a company inventing its own) is what makes scenario analysis results comparable across companies.
other-reporting-standards.example: A bank's climate scenario analysis might explicitly reference the NGFS's 'Below 2°C' and 'Current Policies' scenarios rather than custom in-house projections.

other-reporting-standards.definition: The trend of GRI, ISSB, ESRS and TNFD aligning their frameworks to reduce duplicate reporting.
other-reporting-standards.plainEnglish: The ongoing trend of GRI, ISSB, ESRS, and TNFD aligning their frameworks to reduce the amount of duplicate reporting companies have to do.
other-reporting-standards.whyItMatters: It's the direct response to a genuine problem: a company facing GRI, ESRS, and IFRS S1/S2 all at once used to have to report largely the same underlying facts three separate ways.
other-reporting-standards.example: GRI-ESRS interoperability mapping is one concrete piece of this broader convergence trend.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: Financing and investment that accounts for ESG factors alongside financial return.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: Financing and investment decisions that factor in ESG considerations alongside — not instead of — financial return.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's the broad umbrella term everything else in this module sits under: SFDR, the EU Taxonomy, green bonds, and impact investing are all specific expressions of it.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A bank offering lower interest rates on loans tied to a borrower's emissions-reduction targets is practicing sustainable finance.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: Systematically weighing ESG factors in the financial analysis and valuation of an investment.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: Systematically factoring ESG considerations into the financial analysis and valuation of an investment, not treating them as a separate ethical add-on.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It marks the difference between a fund that screens out 'bad' companies and one that actually prices ESG risk into every valuation it makes.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: An analyst factoring a company's exposure to future carbon pricing directly into its discounted cash flow valuation is practicing ESG integration.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: An investment strategy excluding certain sectors or companies (e.g. weapons, tobacco, fossil fuels).
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: An investment strategy that simply excludes entire sectors or companies — weapons, tobacco, fossil fuels — from a portfolio.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's the oldest and simplest sustainable investing strategy, and a useful contrast to more sophisticated approaches like best-in-class screening or impact investing.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A pension fund excluding all tobacco company stocks from its portfolio, regardless of their individual ESG performance, is using negative screening.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.dontConfuseWith: Best-in-class screening — that selects the top performers within a sector; exclusionary screening removes entire sectors outright.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A strategy focused on a single sustainability theme (e.g. water, renewable energy, gender equality).
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: A strategy that concentrates a portfolio around one specific sustainability theme — water scarcity, renewable energy, gender equality.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It lets an investor target a specific issue they care about directly, rather than applying a broad ESG filter across everything.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A thematic fund focused entirely on renewable energy infrastructure would hold wind, solar, and grid companies, and little else.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A bond whose proceeds are earmarked for environmental projects.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: A bond where the money raised is specifically earmarked for environmental projects.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's the most established sustainable-debt instrument — the direct model that social bonds and sustainability-linked bonds later adapted.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A utility company might issue a green bond specifically to fund a new offshore wind farm.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.dontConfuseWith: Sustainability-linked bond — a green bond earmarks proceeds for specific projects; an SLB ties the bond's terms to company-wide sustainability performance instead.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A bond whose proceeds are specifically earmarked for projects with social impact.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: A bond where the proceeds are specifically earmarked for projects with a social impact, rather than an environmental one.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It extends the green bond model beyond the environment — proof that sustainable debt instruments aren't only about climate.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A social bond might fund affordable housing construction or hospital infrastructure in underserved areas.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.dontConfuseWith: Green bond — a green bond funds environmental projects; a social bond funds projects with social impact.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A score (e.g. from MSCI, Sustainalytics, ISS) summarising a company's ESG performance or risk.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: A score, from an agency like MSCI, Sustainalytics, or ISS, summarising a company's overall ESG performance or risk.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: These ratings drive real capital allocation decisions, which is exactly why rating divergence — different agencies scoring the same company very differently — is such a persistent problem.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: An investor screening a portfolio for ESG quality might filter out any company with a below-average ESG rating from MSCI.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A strategy selecting the top ESG performers within each sector.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: An investment strategy that selects the top ESG performers within each sector, rather than excluding entire sectors outright.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It lets an investor stay exposed to every sector — including carbon-intensive ones — while still favouring the relatively better performers within each.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A best-in-class fund might still hold an oil company, but only the one with the strongest ESG performance among its industry peers.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.dontConfuseWith: Negative/exclusionary screening — that removes whole sectors; best-in-class keeps every sector but picks its top performers.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: Investing with the explicit intent of generating measurable positive social or environmental impact alongside return.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: Investing with the explicit intent of generating a measurable positive social or environmental impact, alongside financial return.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: Intent and measurability are the key words — it's a stricter bar than most ESG strategies, which mainly manage risk rather than deliberately target positive outcomes.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: An impact investor funding a clean water startup would track a specific metric, like the number of people gaining access to clean water, alongside financial return.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A bond whose coupon is tied to achieving pre-agreed sustainability KPIs.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: A bond whose interest rate is tied to whether the issuer hits pre-agreed sustainability targets — miss the target, and the coupon typically rises.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: Unlike a green bond, an SLB doesn't earmark proceeds for anything specific — it's a bet on the issuer's overall sustainability performance, which makes target-setting integrity crucial.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A company might issue an SLB where its interest rate increases by 0.25% if it fails to hit its 2030 emissions-reduction target.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.dontConfuseWith: Green bond — a green bond funds specific projects; an SLB ties financial terms to company-wide performance targets instead.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: Investors using voting and dialogue to influence a company's ESG policy.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: Investors using their voting rights and direct dialogue with management to influence a company's ESG policy, rather than simply buying or selling shares.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's how large investors exercise ESG influence over companies they hold long-term, when simply divesting isn't practical or effective.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A pension fund voting against a company's board nominees over inadequate climate risk oversight is exercising stewardship.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: Double bottom line measures financial and social/environmental return; triple bottom line adds a third, distinct dimension.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: Double bottom line measures financial return plus one other dimension (social or environmental); triple bottom line adds a third, distinct dimension on top.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's a useful reminder that 'bottom line' language isn't standardised — always check exactly how many dimensions a given framework is actually counting.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A fund reporting financial return and carbon impact is using a double bottom line; adding a separate social impact measure would make it triple.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.term: Green Bond Principles (ICMA - International Capital Market Association)
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: Voluntary market guidelines promoting transparency and integrity in green bonds.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: Voluntary market guidelines, published by ICMA, that promote transparency and integrity in how green bonds are issued and reported on.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: They're the informal industry standard most green bonds are measured against, even without any legal requirement to follow them.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: An issuer following the Green Bond Principles would publish an annual report tracking exactly how green bond proceeds were actually spent.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A voluntary, legally anchored EU standard for green bonds, linked to the EU Taxonomy.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: A voluntary but legally anchored EU standard for green bonds, explicitly linked to the EU Taxonomy's definition of environmentally sustainable activities.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's a stricter, legally-defined alternative to the voluntary ICMA Green Bond Principles — using it means proceeds have to fund genuinely Taxonomy-aligned activities.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: An issuer using the EU Green Bond Standard has to ensure its funded projects actually meet EU Taxonomy criteria, not just a general environmental theme.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.dontConfuseWith: Green Bond Principles — those are voluntary market guidelines with no legal anchoring; the EU Green Bond Standard is a stricter, legally defined EU standard tied to the Taxonomy.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A shareholder vote on a company's climate transition plan.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: A shareholder vote specifically on a company's climate transition plan, separate from ordinary say-on-pay votes.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's one of the more direct channels for stewardship on climate specifically, giving shareholders a formal way to register approval or disapproval of climate strategy.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: Shareholders voting on an oil company's climate transition plan at its annual meeting is a say-on-climate vote.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: The phenomenon of different ESG rating agencies assigning widely differing scores to the same company.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: The well-documented phenomenon of different ESG rating agencies assigning meaningfully different scores to the exact same company.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It undermines the credibility of ESG ratings as an objective measure, and is one of the main reasons regulators have started scrutinising rating agencies themselves.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: One agency might rate a car manufacturer highly for its EV transition, while another rates it poorly for its remaining combustion-engine exposure — same company, very different scores.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: Debate over whether weighing ESG factors is compatible with an investor's duty to act in beneficiaries' interests.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: An ongoing debate over whether an investor weighing ESG factors is compatible with their legal duty to act purely in their beneficiaries' financial interests.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's the legal tension underneath much of the ESG-investing debate — some argue ESG factors are themselves financially material, others argue weighing them risks breaching fiduciary duty.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A pension fund trustee might face this exact question when deciding whether excluding fossil fuels serves or conflicts with beneficiaries' financial interests.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: Combining public/philanthropic capital with commercial capital to lower risk and attract private investment into sustainable projects.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: Combining public or philanthropic capital with commercial capital, to lower risk and attract private investment into projects that wouldn't otherwise get funded.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's a key tool for funding sustainable projects in markets too risky for purely commercial capital alone — the public money absorbs some risk to make the deal work.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A development bank might provide a first-loss guarantee that makes a renewable energy project in an emerging market attractive enough for private investors to join.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A Belgian non-profit, active since 1992, that independently verifies sustainable finance products — historically under its own Ethibel Pioneer/Excellence registers, today mainly as a screener for Febelfin's 'Towards Sustainability' label and specific named funds.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: A Belgian non-profit, active since 1992, independently verifying sustainable finance products. It used to run its own Ethibel Pioneer and Ethibel Excellence investment registers, but today its main role is screening applications for Febelfin's 'Towards Sustainability' label, plus verifying specific named funds and products one by one.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's one of the older, established players in Belgian sustainable-finance verification — worth recognising, though its role has shifted from running its own standalone label to screening for other labels like 'Towards Sustainability'.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A Belgian fund manager applying for the 'Towards Sustainability' label has that application screened by Forum Ethibel before the independent Central Labelling Agency makes the final award decision.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A Brussels-based network of national sustainable investment forums that researches and advocates for sustainable finance policy across Europe.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: A Brussels-based network of national sustainable investment forums that researches sustainable finance trends and advocates for related policy across Europe.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's one of the main industry voices shaping European sustainable finance policy discussions, distinct from any single national body.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: Eurosif might publish an annual market study tracking how much European assets under management now fall under sustainable investment strategies.

sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.definition: A Belgian quality label for sustainable financial products, created by Febelfin and awarded by the independent Central Labelling Agency.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.plainEnglish: A Belgian quality label for sustainable financial products, created by the Belgian financial sector federation Febelfin and awarded by an independent Central Labelling Agency.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.whyItMatters: It's a concrete, national example of the kind of third-party sustainability labelling scheme that's grown across Europe alongside SFDR's own EU-wide framework.
sustainable-finance-ethical-investing.example: A Belgian retail investment fund displaying the 'Towards Sustainability' label has been independently reviewed against the label's specific criteria.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: The most widely used global standard for measuring and reporting greenhouse gas emissions.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: The rulebook almost everyone uses to measure and report greenhouse gas emissions, so different companies' numbers can actually be compared.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: Nearly every other framework in this unit — Scope 1/2/3, CSRD's ESRS E1, SBTi — is built on top of the GHG Protocol's definitions, so it's worth knowing first.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: When a company reports its Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions, it's following the GHG Protocol's categories, whether or not the report says so explicitly.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: Direct emissions from sources owned or controlled by the organisation (e.g. company vehicles, factory boilers).
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: Emissions that come directly out of something the company owns or controls — its own vehicles, boilers, factory chimneys.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: It's the easiest emissions category to measure and the one a company has the most direct control over reducing.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A delivery company's Scope 1 emissions are the exhaust from its own delivery vans.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: Scope 2 — Scope 1 is what the company burns itself; Scope 2 is the emissions behind the electricity it buys.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: Indirect emissions from the generation of purchased electricity, steam, heat or cooling.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: Emissions released elsewhere to generate the electricity, heat, steam, or cooling a company buys and uses.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: A company with no smokestacks of its own — an office-based business, say — can still have a large emissions footprint through the power it buys.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: An office building's Scope 2 emissions come from the power plant that generated the electricity running its lights and computers.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: Scope 1 — Scope 1 is burned on-site; Scope 2 is embedded in purchased energy.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: A claim of zero net CO2 emissions, often achieved through offsetting without a mandatory deep reduction beforehand.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: A claim that a company's net CO2 emissions add up to zero — usually reached by offsetting, not necessarily by cutting emissions first.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: It's a weaker, more loosely-defined claim than 'net zero,' and one regulators increasingly scrutinize — see the Green Claims Directive and EmpCo unit.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A company might claim to be carbon neutral this year purely by buying offset certificates, without reducing its own emissions at all.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: Net zero — net zero requires deep emissions cuts first, consistent with a 1.5°C pathway, with offsetting only for what's left; carbon neutral has no such requirement.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: A certificate representing a ton of avoided or compensated CO2 emissions elsewhere.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: A certificate representing one ton of CO2 that was avoided or compensated for somewhere else — often by funding a forest, renewable energy, or efficiency project.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: Offsets let a company claim credit for emissions reductions it didn't make itself, which is exactly why their quality and verification are so contested.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A company might buy offsets from a reforestation project in Brazil to compensate for emissions from its own factory in Germany.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: Carbon removal — an offset can represent avoided emissions elsewhere; removal specifically means CO2 was pulled out of the atmosphere.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: A unit making the warming effect of different greenhouse gases comparable to CO2.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: A common unit that converts the warming effect of different greenhouse gases — methane, nitrous oxide, and others — into an equivalent amount of CO2, so they can be added up on one scale.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: Without it, a company couldn't meaningfully total up emissions from different gases with very different warming potency into one headline number.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A ton of methane has a much larger warming effect than a ton of CO2, so it might be reported as, say, 28 tons of CO2e.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: All other indirect emissions across the value chain, upstream and downstream (often the largest share).
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: Every other indirect emission across the value chain — from the suppliers a company buys from to how customers use and dispose of its products.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: For most companies this is by far the largest slice of their total footprint, and the hardest to measure since it depends on data from outside the company.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: For a car manufacturer, Scope 3 includes emissions from steel suppliers upstream and from drivers burning fuel downstream.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: Scope 1 and 2 — those cover only what the company itself burns or buys as energy; Scope 3 is everything else up and down the chain.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: A state where remaining greenhouse gas emissions are fully offset by removals, after deep reductions consistent with a 1.5 degree pathway.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: A state where any remaining greenhouse gas emissions are fully balanced out by removals, but only after making deep cuts consistent with limiting warming to 1.5°C.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: It's the climate target companies and countries are actually being held to — and 'deep reductions first' is the part loose 'carbon neutral' claims tend to skip.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: An airline pursuing net zero must first cut emissions as far as physically possible before using carbon removal for whatever's left.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: Carbon neutral — a much looser, less rigorously defined claim that doesn't require reductions before offsetting.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: An initiative that validates corporate targets against the level of reduction climate science requires.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: An independent initiative that checks whether a company's emissions-reduction target is actually steep enough to match what climate science says is needed.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: It stops companies from setting vague or convenient climate targets — SBTi validation is a credibility signal that the target isn't just marketing.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A company might announce 'science-based targets validated by the SBTi' to prove its 2030 emissions goal isn't just a nice-sounding number.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: A technique that actually extracts CO2 from the atmosphere (e.g. reforestation, Direct Air Capture).
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: A technique that physically pulls CO2 out of the atmosphere, rather than simply avoiding new emissions — reforestation and Direct Air Capture are examples.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: Only removal, not avoidance-based offsetting, can compensate for the 'residual' emissions left over after a company has cut everything it can under net zero.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A company might fund a Direct Air Capture facility that mechanically extracts CO2 from the air and stores it underground.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: Carbon offset — an offset can represent avoided emissions elsewhere, which is a weaker claim than actual removal.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: A conversion factor turning activity data into CO2-equivalent figures.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: A conversion number that turns an everyday activity — burning a litre of diesel, say — into a CO2-equivalent figure.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: Emission factors are the actual arithmetic behind every Scope 1/2/3 number a company reports; without them, activity data can't become an emissions total.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: Multiplying the litres of diesel a delivery fleet burned by diesel's emission factor gives its Scope 1 emissions in CO2e.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: The European carbon market where companies must buy or receive emission allowances.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: The EU's carbon market, where heavy industry and power companies must hold an allowance for every ton of CO2 they emit — and buy more if they run short.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: It puts a real, tradeable price on carbon for the sectors it covers, giving companies a direct financial incentive to cut emissions.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A steel plant that emits more CO2 than its free allowances cover has to buy additional allowances on the EU ETS market.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: CBAM — CBAM extends a similar carbon cost to imports from outside the EU, specifically to stop companies dodging the EU ETS by moving production abroad.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: Relocating CO2-intensive production to countries with less stringent climate policy.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: When a company shifts CO2-intensive production to a country with weaker climate rules, so the emissions still happen — just somewhere with less regulation.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: It's the loophole that measures like the EU ETS and CBAM are specifically designed to close, so climate policy doesn't just relocate emissions instead of cutting them.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A cement producer might move a plant outside the EU to avoid EU ETS carbon costs — the emissions don't disappear, they just move.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: Physical risk is direct damage from climate change; transition risk is the financial fallout of shifting to a low-carbon economy.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: Two different ways climate change can hit a company financially: physical risk is direct damage from climate events; transition risk is the cost of adapting to a low-carbon economy.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD)-style climate disclosures are built around exactly this split — investors want to know which kind of risk a company is exposed to, and how much.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A coastal factory faces physical risk from flooding, while a coal-fired power plant faces transition risk from stricter carbon regulation making it obsolete.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: A calculation method based on the average emissions intensity of the regional electricity grid.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: A way of calculating Scope 2 emissions using the average emissions intensity of the regional electricity grid a company draws power from.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: Reporting both location-based and market-based Scope 2 side by side (the GHG Protocol's 'dual reporting' requirement) stops a company from hiding a dirty local grid behind clean-energy certificates.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A factory on a coal-heavy grid gets a high location-based Scope 2 figure, even if it separately buys renewable energy certificates.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: Scope 2 market-based — that method instead reflects the specific energy contracts and certificates a company has bought.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: A calculation method based on specific energy contracts and certificates (e.g. Guarantees of Origin).
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: A way of calculating Scope 2 emissions based on the specific energy a company has contracted for — including renewable energy certificates — rather than the grid average.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: It lets a company show the effect of actively buying renewable power, but it can also make emissions look lower than the electricity it actually draws locally.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A company buying Guarantees of Origin for wind power can report a near-zero market-based Scope 2 figure, even on a coal-heavy grid.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: Scope 2 location-based — that method reflects the actual regional grid mix, regardless of any certificates purchased.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: A carbon border tax on imports from outside the EU to prevent carbon leakage.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: An EU carbon charge applied to certain imports from outside the EU, so foreign producers face roughly the same carbon cost as EU companies under the EU ETS.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: It's the EU's answer to carbon leakage — without it, companies could dodge EU carbon costs simply by importing instead of producing domestically.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A non-EU steel exporter selling into the EU has to account for the carbon emitted making that steel, under CBAM.
climate-carbon-accounting.dontConfuseWith: EU ETS — the ETS prices carbon for production inside the EU; CBAM extends a comparable cost to imports.

climate-carbon-accounting.definition: A notional price per ton of CO2 a company uses internally to steer investment decisions.
climate-carbon-accounting.plainEnglish: A notional cost per ton of CO2 that a company applies to its own decisions internally, even where no law requires it to pay anything.
climate-carbon-accounting.whyItMatters: It lets a company steer investment decisions — like whether to build a new plant — by baking in the future cost of carbon before regulation forces the issue.
climate-carbon-accounting.example: A company might reject an otherwise profitable factory expansion because, at its internal carbon price of €80/ton, the project's emissions make it unattractive.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: An economic model aimed at retaining the value of materials and products through reuse, repair and recycling.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: An economic model built around keeping materials and products in use for as long as possible — through reuse, repair, and recycling — instead of throwing them away.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: It's the positive framework climate and resource policy is steering toward, and shows up throughout EU sustainability regulation as a stated goal.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A furniture company designing products to be disassembled and refurbished, rather than replaced, is operating a circular economy model.
circular-economy-biodiversity.dontConfuseWith: Linear economy — the traditional model this concept is defined against.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: The traditional 'take-make-waste' model the circular economy pushes against.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: The traditional 'take, make, waste' model: resources get extracted, turned into a product, used once, and thrown away.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: It's the default the circular economy is trying to replace — knowing the term helps you spot when a company's practices are still linear despite circular language.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A fast-fashion brand producing cheap clothing designed to be worn briefly and discarded is a textbook example of a linear economy.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: The leading non-profit advancing the global transition to a circular economy.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: The leading non-profit organization pushing the global shift toward a circular economy.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: Many circular-economy concepts and measurement tools that show up in corporate reporting — including the Material Circularity Indicator — originate from this one organization.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A company's circularity report might cite the Ellen MacArthur Foundation's framework as the basis for its methodology.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: The stock of natural resources and ecosystem services on which economic activity depends.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: The stock of natural resources — forests, soil, water, minerals — and the ecosystems built on them, that economic activity ultimately depends on.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: Framing nature as 'capital' — an asset that can be depleted, like financial capital — is what lets investors and regulators start treating biodiversity loss as a genuine financial risk.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A company's supply chain that depends on stable rainfall for its crops is drawing on natural capital, whether that's counted anywhere on its balance sheet or not.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: The benefits nature provides to people (e.g. pollination, water purification, climate regulation).
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: The concrete benefits nature provides to people and business — pollination, clean water, flood protection, climate regulation.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: These services are usually free and invisible until they break down — a company only notices the value of pollinators once bee populations collapse and crop yields fall.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A coffee grower depends on the ecosystem service of pollination by wild bees, without paying anything for it directly.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: The decline in the variety of species and ecosystems, recognised as a financial risk under ESRS E4 and TNFD.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: The ongoing decline in the variety of species and ecosystems across the planet.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: It's now formally recognized as a financial risk, not just an environmental one — both ESRS E4 (European Sustainability Reporting Standards, under CSRD) and TNFD (Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures) require companies to assess and disclose their exposure to it.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A food company reliant on a single wild fish stock faces real financial risk if biodiversity loss causes that stock to collapse.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: The principle that producers remain responsible for a product's environmental impact after sale, including its waste phase.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: The principle that a producer stays responsible for a product's environmental impact even after it's sold — including what happens to it as waste.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: It shifts the cost of dealing with waste back onto the company that created it, giving a direct financial incentive to design longer-lasting, more recyclable products.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A packaging producer required under EPR rules to fund the collection and recycling of its own packaging waste.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: EU legislation requiring member states to restore degraded ecosystems.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: EU legislation requiring member states to actively restore degraded ecosystems — not just stop further damage, but reverse some of it.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: It's one of the concrete legal obligations behind the EU's broader biodiversity ambitions, and can create restoration requirements that touch land companies operate on or depend on.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A member state might be required under this law to restore a percentage of its degraded wetlands by a set deadline.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: A measurement method (Ellen MacArthur Foundation) quantifying how circular a product or company is.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: A measurement tool, developed by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, that scores how circular a specific product or company actually is.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: It turns the fuzzy idea of 'circularity' into a comparable number, so a circularity claim can be checked rather than taken on faith.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A company might report a Material Circularity Indicator score for a product line to show how much of it is genuinely reused or recycled material.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: A design philosophy where products are designed so materials fully return to a biological or technical cycle after use.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: A design philosophy where a product is built from the start so its materials can fully return to either a biological cycle (compost) or a technical cycle (recycling) once it's done being used.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: It's a stricter design standard than ordinary recyclability — it asks whether a product was ever designed with its end-of-life in mind at all.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A cradle-to-cradle-designed carpet might use materials that can be fully broken down and remade into a new carpet at the end of its life.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: An EU regulation requiring companies to prove products (e.g. cocoa, soy, timber) don't come from deforested land.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: An EU regulation requiring companies to prove that products like cocoa, soy, coffee, and timber weren't grown on land that was deforested after a set cutoff date.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: It puts a hard, traceable compliance requirement on supply chains that were previously very difficult to verify — a company can't sell these products in the EU without proof.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A chocolate company must be able to trace its cocoa back to the specific plot of land it was grown on to comply with EUDR.

circular-economy-biodiversity.definition: The extent to which business activities and profit rely on healthy ecosystems, core to TNFD analysis.
circular-economy-biodiversity.plainEnglish: How much a business's operations and profits actually rely on healthy, functioning ecosystems.
circular-economy-biodiversity.whyItMatters: It's the core question TNFD (Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures) analysis is built around — a company can't manage a nature-related risk it hasn't first recognized it depends on.
circular-economy-biodiversity.example: A beverage company is highly nature-dependent on clean, reliable freshwater sources — a risk that's easy to overlook until a drought hits.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: An umbrella term for slavery, human trafficking, forced labour and child labour.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: An umbrella term covering slavery, human trafficking, forced labour, and child labour — the most severe human rights abuses a supply chain can contain.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: It's the term that shows up in supply-chain law and due diligence obligations (like CSDDD) as the worst-case scenario a company must actively check it isn't funding.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A clothing brand's supply-chain audit checking for modern slavery would look for signs of trafficking, debt bondage, or underage workers at its factories.
social-issues-human-rights.dontConfuseWith: Forced labour — forced labour is one specific form modern slavery takes; modern slavery is the broader umbrella covering several related abuses.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: Work that harms a child's development, health or schooling.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: Work that harms a child's development, health, or ability to go to school — not all work by young people counts, but exploitative or hazardous work does.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: It's one of the specific abuses supply-chain due diligence laws require companies to actively screen for, not just avoid causing directly.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A cocoa supplier found to be using children in hazardous farm work instead of sending them to school would be a child labour violation.
social-issues-human-rights.dontConfuseWith: Modern slavery — child labour is one specific form the broader umbrella term covers.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: Consultation between employers, worker representatives and government over working conditions.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: Structured consultation between employers, worker representatives, and sometimes government, over working conditions and workplace decisions.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: Genuine social dialogue is treated as a marker of a healthy labour relationship, and its presence or absence is something CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) / ESRS S1 (European Sustainability Reporting Standards) reporting increasingly asks about.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A company negotiating a restructuring plan with a works council, rather than announcing it unilaterally, is engaging in social dialogue.
social-issues-human-rights.dontConfuseWith: Freedom of association — that's the underlying right to organise; social dialogue is the actual conversation that right makes possible.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: Policy aimed at diversity, equity and inclusion within an organisation.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: Company policy aimed at building a genuinely diverse workforce, treating people equitably, and making sure everyone actually feels included, not just present.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: It's one of the most visible social-pillar programs a company runs, and increasingly shows up in ESRS S1 workforce reporting metrics like pay gaps and board diversity.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A company's DEI program might include blind CV screening, pay-equity audits, and mentorship programs for underrepresented groups.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: A (often third-party) assessment of working conditions at a supplier against a code of conduct.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: An on-the-ground assessment — often by an independent third party — of actual working conditions at a supplier, checked against a code of conduct.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: It's the practical, verification side of human rights due diligence — a company's supplier code of conduct is only as good as the audits that check whether it's actually followed.
social-issues-human-rights.example: An auditor visiting a garment factory unannounced to interview workers and check safety conditions is conducting a social audit.
social-issues-human-rights.dontConfuseWith: Human rights impact assessment — a social audit checks compliance at one supplier site; an HRIA is a broader assessment of a project's or activity's human rights effects.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: The process of identifying and addressing risks of human rights violations in own operations and the value chain.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: The ongoing process of identifying, preventing, and addressing human rights risks in a company's own operations and its entire value chain.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: It's the core obligation behind CSDDD and similar laws — not a one-off check, but a continuous process a company has to keep running.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A company mapping which of its suppliers operate in regions with high forced-labour risk, and building a plan to address it, is conducting human rights due diligence.
social-issues-human-rights.dontConfuseWith: Human rights impact assessment (HRIA) — an HRIA is typically a specific, bounded assessment (e.g. for one project); due diligence is the broader, ongoing process it feeds into.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: Work performed under coercion or threat of penalty, without voluntary consent.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: Work someone is coerced into doing, under threat of penalty, without having genuinely and voluntarily agreed to it.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: It's the specific abuse the EU Forced Labour Regulation directly targets, banning products made with it from the EU market outright.
social-issues-human-rights.example: Workers unable to leave a job because their employer confiscated their passports are in a forced labour situation.
social-issues-human-rights.dontConfuseWith: Modern slavery — forced labour is one specific form modern slavery takes.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: Income that provides a worker and their family a decent standard of living, often higher than the statutory minimum wage.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: Enough income for a worker and their family to actually afford a decent standard of living — often well above the legal statutory minimum wage.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: Paying the legal minimum wage doesn't automatically mean workers can afford to live decently — living wage is the higher bar social-impact reporting increasingly asks about.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A garment worker earning the legal minimum wage in their country might still fall short of a living wage if that minimum doesn't cover basic food and housing costs.
social-issues-human-rights.dontConfuseWith: Statutory minimum wage — the living wage is a needs-based benchmark, often calculated independently and set higher than whatever the law requires.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: Workers' right to organise and bargain collectively.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: Workers' right to organise themselves — forming or joining a union — and to bargain collectively with their employer.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: It's a foundational labour right referenced across nearly every human-rights framework (International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions, the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs), and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises) as a baseline that due diligence must protect.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A supplier that fires workers for attempting to organise a union would be violating freedom of association.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: The difference in pay between groups of employees (e.g. gender pay gap), a disclosure required under ESRS S1 (European Sustainability Reporting Standards) where workforce topics are assessed as material.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: The difference in pay between groups of employees — most commonly reported between genders.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: It's a quantitative disclosure required under ESRS S1 once workforce is assessed as a material topic, turning what used to be an internal HR matter into a public, comparable metric.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A company might report a 12% gender pay gap in its CSRD sustainability statement, calculated as the average pay difference between men and women.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: The principle that the shift to a sustainable economy must be fair, protecting jobs and communities dependent on fossil sectors.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: The principle that the shift to a sustainable, low-carbon economy has to be fair — protecting the jobs and communities that currently depend on fossil-fuel industries.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: Climate policy that ignores this risk creates exactly the social backlash that ends up slowing climate action down — it makes the social and environmental pillars inseparable.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A government funding retraining programs for coal miners as mines close, rather than just letting the region collapse economically, is pursuing a just transition.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: A channel through which local residents or affected communities, not just employees, can raise complaints about business impact.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: A channel that lets local residents or affected communities — not just a company's own employees — raise complaints about how a business affects them.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: Human rights due diligence has to cover harm to outside communities too, not just the workforce, and this is the mechanism that lets those affected actually be heard.
social-issues-human-rights.example: Villagers near a mine using a community-level grievance mechanism to report water contamination they believe the mine caused.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: The right of indigenous communities to give informed consent in advance for projects on their land.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: The right of indigenous communities to give — or withhold — informed consent before a project goes ahead on their land, with enough time and information to decide freely.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: Projects that skip FPIC are a recurring source of major human rights controversies and reputational damage in extractives, agriculture, and infrastructure.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A company planning a dam on indigenous land is expected to secure FPIC from the affected community before construction begins, not after.

social-issues-human-rights.definition: A systematic assessment of the actual and potential human rights impact of a project or business activity.
social-issues-human-rights.plainEnglish: A systematic study of the actual and potential human rights effects of a specific project or business activity.
social-issues-human-rights.whyItMatters: It's the analytical tool that feeds into human rights due diligence — you need to have assessed the impact before you can meaningfully address it.
social-issues-human-rights.example: A company might commission an HRIA before starting a new mining project to identify which local communities could be affected and how.
social-issues-human-rights.dontConfuseWith: Human rights due diligence — an HRIA is typically a specific, one-off assessment; due diligence is the broader, continuous process it feeds into.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: The system of rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: The system of rules, practices, and processes by which a company is directed and controlled — who decides what, and who holds them accountable.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: It's the 'G' in ESG, and everything else in this module — board diversity, say-on-pay, whistleblower protection — is a specific piece of it.
governance-anti-corruption.example: A company's corporate governance includes how its board is structured, how executives are held accountable, and how shareholders can exercise their rights.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: Internal policy aimed at preventing bribery and corruption, a mandatory element of ESRS G1 (the European Sustainability Reporting Standards' 'Business conduct' section).
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: A company's internal policy specifically aimed at preventing bribery and corruption.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: It's a mandatory element of ESRS G1 reporting under the CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) — a company can't simply claim to be against corruption, it has to show the policy exists.
governance-anti-corruption.example: An anti-corruption policy might explicitly ban facilitation payments and require gifts above a certain value to be logged and disclosed.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: Diversity within the board of directors or supervisory board, often reported as a quantitative indicator.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: How diverse a company's board of directors or supervisory board actually is — across gender, background, and often other dimensions.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: It's one of the most commonly quoted, quantifiable ESG governance indicators — easy to headline, but only one piece of genuine board effectiveness.
governance-anti-corruption.example: A company might report that 40% of its board members are women as its board diversity figure.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: The degree to which senior management models ethical standards and compliance through its own behaviour.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: How much senior management's own behaviour actually models the ethical standards and compliance culture the company claims to have.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: A code of conduct is only as credible as the leadership that's seen following it — auditors and investors treat weak tone at the top as a governance red flag.
governance-anti-corruption.example: A CEO who publicly champions ethics but privately pressures staff to hit targets by any means is undermining tone at the top.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: Two-tier separates management and oversight into two bodies; one-tier combines executive and non-executive directors on one board.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: Two different board structures: a two-tier system splits management and oversight into two separate bodies; a one-tier system puts executive and non-executive directors together on a single board.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: Governance expectations and reporting norms differ by jurisdiction partly because of this split — Germany traditionally uses two-tier, the UK and US typically one-tier.
governance-anti-corruption.example: A German company with a separate Vorstand (management board) and Aufsichtsrat (supervisory board) is using a two-tier structure.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: Shareholders' voting right on executive remuneration policy.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: Shareholders' right to vote on a company's executive remuneration policy.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: It gives investors a direct, formal check on executive pay — a governance mechanism that's grown more common and more binding across markets.
governance-anti-corruption.example: Shareholders voting down a proposed executive bonus scheme at an annual general meeting is a say-on-pay vote in action.
governance-anti-corruption.dontConfuseWith: ESG-linked executive pay — say-on-pay is the shareholders' voting right itself; ESG-linked pay is one possible design of the compensation package being voted on.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: An EU directive mandating reporting channels and protection for whistleblowers.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: An EU directive requiring companies to set up reporting channels for whistleblowers and legally protecting them from retaliation.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: It turns whistleblower protection from a matter of internal company policy into a binding legal requirement across the EU.
governance-anti-corruption.example: A company setting up an anonymous internal hotline for reporting misconduct, as legally required, is complying with the Whistleblower Directive.
governance-anti-corruption.dontConfuseWith: Whistleblower — the directive is the EU law; a whistleblower is the person the law protects.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: The UN Global Compact's ten principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: Ten principles set out by the UN Global Compact, covering human rights, labour standards, environmental protection, and anti-corruption.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: It's one of the earliest and most widely-signed voluntary corporate sustainability commitments, and many later frameworks build on the same four areas.
governance-anti-corruption.example: A company that has signed the UN Global Compact commits to align its strategy with all ten principles, including not being complicit in human rights abuses.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: A practice tying part of executive remuneration to achieving ESG targets.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: A pay structure that ties part of an executive's compensation directly to hitting specific ESG targets, not just financial ones.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: It's one of the clearest signals of whether ESG commitments are backed by real incentives, or are just messaging — money tends to concentrate attention.
governance-anti-corruption.example: A CEO's bonus might be reduced if the company misses its annual emissions-reduction target, under an ESG-linked pay structure.
governance-anti-corruption.dontConfuseWith: Say-on-pay — that's the shareholders' voting right; ESG-linked pay is a specific design choice for the pay package itself.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: Shareholders using votes, resolutions or public pressure to influence a company's strategy or conduct.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: Shareholders using their votes, formal resolutions, or public pressure to try to influence a company's strategy or conduct.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: It's one of the main ways ESG pressure actually reaches company boards from the outside — an activist investor can force a climate or governance issue onto the agenda.
governance-anti-corruption.example: A group of investors filing a shareholder resolution demanding the company disclose its lobbying spend is an act of shareholder activism.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: Disclosure of the amounts and topics involved in influencing legislation, required under ESRS G1.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: Disclosing how much a company spends on lobbying and which issues it's trying to influence in legislation.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: It's a required ESRS G1 disclosure under CSRD, and a common area where a company's public ESG messaging can quietly contradict its private political spending.
governance-anti-corruption.example: A company might publicly support stronger climate policy while its lobbying disclosure shows it funded efforts to weaken a specific climate law.

governance-anti-corruption.definition: An ESRS G1 indicator measuring how quickly a company pays its (especially smaller) suppliers.
governance-anti-corruption.plainEnglish: An ESRS G1 indicator measuring how quickly a company actually pays its suppliers, especially smaller ones.
governance-anti-corruption.whyItMatters: Slow payment terms can quietly squeeze small suppliers' cash flow — this metric turns a previously invisible practice into a disclosed governance indicator.
governance-anti-corruption.example: A large retailer disclosing that it takes 90 days on average to pay small suppliers, versus 30 days for large ones, under its supplier payment terms reporting.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.definition: Exaggerating, fabricating or under-substantiating environmental claims to create a greener image than is warranted.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.plainEnglish: Exaggerating, inventing, or failing to properly back up an environmental claim, to make a company or product look greener than it really is.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.whyItMatters: It's the umbrella problem the entire EmpCo/UCPD/Green Claims regulatory push exists to stop — nearly every term in this module is a specific rule targeting one form of it.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.example: A company labelling a product 'eco-friendly' with no evidence behind the claim, purely because the packaging is a certain shade of green, is greenwashing.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.definition: A vague claim (e.g. 'eco-friendly') banned under EmpCo unless the company can demonstrate recognised excellent environmental performance relevant to the claim — general substantiation on its own is not enough.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.plainEnglish: A vague claim — like 'eco-friendly' or 'green' — made without proof of genuinely excellent environmental performance behind it.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.whyItMatters: EmpCo sets a specific, high bar here: the claim is only allowed if the company can show recognised excellent environmental performance relevant to that claim — in practice usually compliance with the EU Ecolabel (Regulation 66/2010) or an officially recognised ISO 14024-type ecolabelling scheme. Ordinary 'we have some data behind this' substantiation does not clear that bar.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.example: A cleaning product labelled simply 'environmentally friendly,' with no EU Ecolabel or equivalent recognised certification behind it, is a generic environmental claim EmpCo now prohibits — even if the company has some internal data supporting it.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.dontConfuseWith: Sustainability label — a label is permitted precisely because it's tied to an official certification scheme; a generic claim has no such backing.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.definition: Words like 'green', 'sustainable', 'eco-friendly' used without quantitative backing, carrying heightened enforcement risk.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.plainEnglish: Words like 'green,' 'sustainable,' or 'eco-friendly' used in marketing without quantitative evidence behind them.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.whyItMatters: These specific words are now flagged as carrying heightened enforcement risk — using them casually in marketing copy has real regulatory consequences post-EmpCo.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.example: A marketing team drafting copy that says a product is simply 'sustainable,' with no data to back it, is using a recognised greenwashing trigger word.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.definition: 'Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition': bans specific misleading environmental and sustainability practices.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.plainEnglish: Short for 'Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition' — an EU directive that bans a specific list of misleading environmental and sustainability marketing practices.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.whyItMatters: Its national rules become applicable across the EU from 27 September 2026 — this is the concrete law behind most of the specific bans in this module (generic claims, unbacked carbon-neutral claims, and more).
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.example: A company's marketing team reviewing its product claims ahead of the EmpCo deadline would check each one against the directive's specific list of banned practices.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.definition: The broader EU directive on unfair commercial practices that EmpCo builds on.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.plainEnglish: The broader, older EU directive on unfair commercial practices in general, which EmpCo builds directly on top of.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.whyItMatters: EmpCo doesn't stand alone — it's an amendment adding specific environmental-claim rules onto this pre-existing consumer protection framework.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.example: A misleading environmental claim could be challenged both as a specific EmpCo violation and as a broader UCPD unfair commercial practice.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.dontConfuseWith: EmpCo Directive — EmpCo is the newer, environment-specific addition; UCPD is the broader pre-existing framework it amends.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.definition: A claim that a product is more environmentally friendly than a competitor or previous version; requires verifiable, objective substantiation.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.plainEnglish: A claim that a product is more environmentally friendly than a competitor's product, or than an earlier version of itself — requiring verifiable, objective evidence to back it up.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.whyItMatters: Comparisons invite an obvious question — 'compared to what, exactly?' — and EmpCo now requires a real, checkable answer, not just an assertion.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.example: A company claiming its new packaging uses '30% less plastic than our previous version' needs objective, verifiable data behind that specific number.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.definition: A claim about future sustainability goals; permitted under EmpCo only with a concrete, time-bound implementation plan.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.plainEnglish: A claim about a future sustainability goal — permitted under EmpCo only if backed by a concrete, time-bound implementation plan, not just an aspiration.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.whyItMatters: It closes a common greenwashing loophole: promising a distant future target with no real plan to get there, and getting credit for it today regardless.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.example: A company claiming it 'will be carbon neutral by 2040' now has to show a concrete, time-bound plan for how it intends to get there, not just state the goal.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.definition: The requirement that every environmental claim be backed by verifiable, up-to-date evidence.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.plainEnglish: The requirement that every environmental claim be backed by verifiable, up-to-date evidence — not outdated data or unverifiable assertions.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.whyItMatters: It's the underlying test almost every other rule in this module ultimately comes down to: can the company actually prove what it's claiming?
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.example: A company claiming its product is 'recyclable' needs current, verifiable evidence — not a five-year-old study that no longer reflects reality.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.definition: Permitted under EmpCo only if based on an official certification scheme or established by a public authority.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.plainEnglish: A sustainability label is only permitted under EmpCo if it's based on an official certification scheme, or established by a public authority — not a company's own invented badge.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.whyItMatters: It closes off a common workaround: companies designing their own official-looking green logo with no actual certification body behind it.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.example: An EU Ecolabel is a legitimate sustainability label under EmpCo; a company's own self-designed leaf icon with no certifying body behind it is not.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.dontConfuseWith: Generic environmental claim — a generic claim has no label or scheme at all; this term is specifically about when a label itself is legitimate.

greenwashing-empco-ucpd.definition: Deliberately staying silent about sustainability performance for fear of criticism or legal risk - the mirror image of greenwashing.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.plainEnglish: Deliberately staying quiet about genuine sustainability performance, out of fear of criticism, scrutiny, or legal risk.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.whyItMatters: It's the mirror image of greenwashing, and an unintended side effect of tighter claims regulation — some companies now under-report real progress rather than risk making a claim that gets challenged.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.example: A company that quietly hits a real emissions target but stops mentioning it publicly, worried any claim might draw greenwashing scrutiny, is greenhushing.
greenwashing-empco-ucpd.dontConfuseWith: Greenwashing — greenwashing overstates sustainability performance; greenhushing understates or hides genuine performance.
